The Ericsson share purchase plan (ESPP)
Ericsson is committed to helping employees thrive and to recognizing them 
for the impact they create by providing opportunities to enrich their working 
experience. In order to encourage employees to play an active role in achiev-
ing the Company’s purpose, further create sense of belonging and ownership, 
the Ericsson share purchase plan is offered. At the end of 2025 the plan is 
implemented in 72 countries to 73,879 eligible employees.
The ESPP is an all-employee share purchase plan that enables employees 
to purchase Ericsson B-shares up to a maximum value of SEK 55,000 per 
year via monthly payroll deduction. In recognition of the employees’ commit-
ment, Ericsson supports the participants with a net cash payment up to 15% 
of their elected contribution amounts and will cover the tax on the Company 
supported amount, which is payable via payroll. Under the ESPP participants 
will acquire Ericsson B shares at market price on the stock exchange and the 
ESPP does therefore not have any dilutive effect.

P1   Material accounting policies 
The financial statements of the Parent Company, Telefonaktiebolaget  
LM Ericsson, have been prepared in accordance with the Annual Accounts 
Act and RFR 2 ”Reporting in separate financial statements.” RFR 2 requires 
the Parent Company to use the same accounting principles as for the Group, 
i.e., IFRS, to the extent allowed by RFR 2. 
The main deviations between accounting policies adopted for the Group 
and accounting policies for the Parent Company are:
Subsidiaries and associated companies 
The investments are accounted for according to the acquisition cost method. 
Investments are carried at cost and only dividends are accounted for in the 
income statement. An annual impairment test of the investments in subsid-
iaries and associated companies is performed in the fourth quarter, or when 
there is an indication of impairment. An impairment loss is recognized if the 
carrying amount of an investment exceeds the sum of the subsidiary’s equity 
and related goodwill, intangible liabilities and deferred tax liabilities or its 
estimated future cash flows after tax. Cash flows are discounted to present 
value using an after-tax discount rate that reflects current market assess-
ments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the asset. 
Contributions to/from subsidiaries and shareholders’ contributions are 
accounted for according to RFR 2. Contributions from/to Swedish subsid-
iaries are reported net in the income statement. Shareholders’ contributions 
increase the Parent Company’s investments. 
Classification and measurement of financial instruments
IFRS 9 ”Financial instruments” is adopted, except regarding financial  
guarantees and revaluation of borrowings due to change in credit risk. 
Financial guarantees are included in contingent liabilities in accordance with 
the exemption allowed in RFR 2. Revaluation of borrowings due to change  
in credit risk is reported in the income statement. 
Leases
Leases are reported according to the exemption allowed in RFR 2. For leases 
where the Parent Company is lessee this means that the right-of-use assets 
and lease liabilities are not recognized on the balance sheet. Costs under the 
lease are recognized in the income statement on a straight-line basis over 
the term of the lease. Lease incentives received are recognized as an integral 
part of the total lease expense, over the term of the lease. For leases where 
the Parent Company is lessor, the equipment is recorded as property, plant 
and equipment and revenue and depreciation are recognized on a straight-
line basis over the lease term. Expenses related to the lease income are  
recognized when incurred. Direct expenses incurred when a lease agree-
ment is entered are added to the carrying amount of the leased asset and 
expensed over the lease period on the same basis as the lease income. 
Deferred taxes
The accounting of untaxed reserves in the balance sheet results in different 
accounting of deferred taxes as compared to the principles applied in the 
consolidated statements. Swedish GAAP and tax regulations require a  
company to report certain differences between the tax basis and book value 
as an untaxed reserve in the balance sheet of the stand-alone financial  
statements. Changes to these reserves are reported as an addition to, or 
withdrawal from, untaxed reserves in the income statement.
Pensions
Pensions are accounted for according to the simplification rule in RFR 2.  
The pension obligation is secured by transferring of funds to a pension trust. 
A net pension obligation is only accounted for to the extent that the  
fair value of the trust is lower than the pension obligation. According to  
RFR 2, disclosures under IAS 19 are adopted as applicable.
Business combinations
Transaction costs attributable to the acquisition are included in the cost  
of acquisition in the Parent Company statements compared to Group  
statements where these costs are expensed as incurred.
Judgments and critical accounting estimates
See notes to the consolidated financial statements – note A2 ”Judgments 
and critical accounting estimates.” Major judgments and critical accounting 
estimates applicable to the Parent Company include provisions and 
contingent liabilities, and acquired intellectual property rights and other  
intangible assets (excluding goodwill).
Changes in accounting policies 
For current and upcoming changes in IFRS standards, details can be found 
in the consolidated financial statements, note A1 ”Material accounting 
policies”. Only additions and exemptions in RFR 2 established by the 
Swedish Corporate Reporting Board (”Rådet för hållbarhets- och finansiell 
rapportering”) are listed below: 
Amendments issued by IASB with effective date January 1, 2025:
There are no additions or exemptions in RFR 2
Amendments issued by IASB with effective date January 1, 2026:
There are no additions or exemptions in RFR 2
New standard with effective date January 1, 2027:
In April 2024, the IASB issued a new standard, IFRS 18, which will replace 
IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements. The standard impacts the 
presentation and disclosures in the financial statements, with the most 
significant impact on the income statement.  
For the Parent Company, applying IFRS 18’s income statement presentation 
requirements is not possible within the framework of the Swedish Annual 
Accounts Act. Accordingly, and in line with exemptions established in RFR 2, 
no major changes—or restatement requirements—to the presentation of the 
income statement are expected.
Any additional recommendations from the Swedish Corporate Reporting 
Board will be followed closely, and any implications will be assessed.
There are no more upcoming standards or changes in standards with material 
impact on the Parent Company.

P14   Post-employment benefits 
The Parent Company has two types of pension plans:
	
– Defined contribution plans: post-employment benefit plans where the 
Parent Company pays fixed contributions into separate entities and  
has no legal or constructive obligation to pay further contributions if the  
entities do not hold sufficient assets to pay all employee benefits relating 
to employee service. The expenses for defined contribution plans are  
recognized during the period when the employee provides service.
	
– Defined benefit plans: post-employment benefit plans where the Parent 
Company’s undertaking is to provide predetermined benefits that the 
employee will receive on or after retirement.

Sustainability Statement
Basis of preparation 
Ericsson’s Sustainability Statement presents 
information on material environmental, social 
and business conduct-related impacts, risks 
and opportunities, together with the govern-
ance, policies, actions, targets and metrics 
used to manage and measure them. Unless 
otherwise stated, the information and data 
refer to the ﬁscal year 2025 (January 1–
December 31).
Reporting scope and boundaries 
The Sustainability Statement has been pre­
pared on a consolidated basis for the Ericsson 
Group, comprising the Parent Company, 
 Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson, and its 
 subsidiaries as presented in Note P8 to the 
Parent Company’s ﬁnancial statements. 
 Environmental and social data from associ­
ated companies or joint ventures over which 
Ericsson does not have operational control 
is not included.
The Sustainability Statement includes 
 disclosures covering the Company’s upstream 
and downstream value chain, including sup­
pliers, vendors, customers and other busi­
ness partners. Focus is placed on the value 
chain for network equipment manufacturing, 
deployment, use and end-of-life treatment, 
where the most material impacts, risks and 
opportunities have been identiﬁed.
Reporting principles and 
disclosures  covered
The Sustainability Statement has been pre­
pared in accordance with the Swedish Annual 
Accounts Act, the European Sustainability 
Reporting Standards (ESRS) and the EU 
 Taxonomy Regulation. It also incorporates 
relevant disclosures from the Sustainability 
Accounting Standards Board’s (SASB) 
 standard for Hardware Manufacturers in 
the  Technology and Communication sector.
A list of the ESRS disclosure requirements 
covered is provided in Appendix 1. Ericsson 
partly applies the phase-in provisions per­
mitted under the ESRS, as set out in the same 
appendix. As part of this phased approach, 
the Company has not yet prepared dis­
closures fully in accordance with ESRS S2 
(Workers in the value chain), S3 (Affected 
communities) and S4 (Consumers and end 
users), but provides information in respect of 
these standards that is broadly aligned with 
their disclosure requirements. This includes 
the minimum information required during 
the phase-in period, where relevant to the 
Company’s material impacts, risks and oppor­
tunities. Further details can be found in each 
respective section. 
Data points derived from other EU legis­
lation that are addressed within the Sustain­
ability Statement are listed in Appendix 2.
The selection of disclosures is based on 
Ericsson’s double materiality assessment, 
applying professional judgment to determine 
which ESRS requirements and entity-speciﬁc 
information are material for users of sustain­
ability statements. The objective is to provide 
a faithful representation of how material 
impacts, risks and opportunities are identi­
ﬁed, managed and measured. No disclosures 
have been omitted on the grounds of intel­
lectual property, know-how or the results of 
innovation. 
Part of the information required under 
ESRS 2 SBM-1, in particular information on 
signiﬁcant products and services offered 
and markets served, is incorporated into 
the Sustainability Statement through cross- 
references to other parts of the Board of 
Directors’ Report.
Statement on due diligence
Appendix 3 provides references to the sections 
of the Sustainability Statement that describe 
how Ericsson applies the core elements of 
due diligence in relation to people and the 
environment.
Time horizons
When assessing impacts, short-, medium- 
and long-term time horizons are deﬁned as 
up to one year, one to ﬁve years and more 
than ﬁve years, respectively. For risks and 
opportunities, the corresponding time frames 
are up to one year, one to two years, and up 
to three years, consistent with the Company’s 
Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) frame­
work. For climate-related scenario analyses, 
longer time horizons are applied as speciﬁed 
in the relevant disclosures.
These time frames support the prepara­
tion of disclosures that are based on infor­
mation that can be assessed with reasonable 
certainty. While some degree of estimation 
is inherent to forward-looking assessments, 
Ericsson aims to ensure that the reported 
information remains reasonably reliable 
and reﬂective of foreseeable conditions.

Methodologies for measurement and data

ity information. 
The Sustainability Statement also includes

Current and anticipated financial effects
As a general principle, current and anticipated 
financial effects related to material impacts, 
risks and opportunities are disclosed when 
they can be identified with reasonable reli-
ability and are considered material. Costs or 
investments that are non-material, or form 
part of the normal course of business, are 
not disclosed separately. The disclosure of 
anticipated financial effects is subject to the 
availability and maturity of methodologies, 
assumptions and data, and will be expanded 
over time in line with applicable ESRS transi-
tional provisions.

Business model
Ericsson is a multinational company head-
quartered in Stockholm, Sweden, serving 
customers in more than 175 countries. The 
company provides hardware, software and 
services for information and communications 
technology (ICT) infrastructure. Its main 
inputs are electronic components, software 
and skilled labor. Its principal outputs are 
network infrastructure, software and services. 
Ericsson’s offerings create value by enabling 
mobile and fixed connectivity, which supports 
communication, economic activity and digital 
services for businesses, end users and society. 
Operations are organized into three pri-
mary business segments: Networks, Cloud 
Software and Services, and Enterprise, and 
an additional fourth ”Other” segment. Those 
are further described in the Board of Directors’ 
Report, sections Business results – Segments 
and Business results – Market Areas (pages 
17–19).

approximately 89 (94) thousand people

Value chain
Ericsson’s value chain spans the extraction 
and processing of raw materials used in elec-
tronic components to the delivery of commu-
nication services for end users. It comprises 
five main stages: global electronics manufac-
turing, direct suppliers, own operations, direct 
customers, and consumers and end users.
As is typical for large multinational com-
panies, Ericsson’s value chain is complex and 
interconnected, which creates challenges 
for visibility and traceability beyond the first 
tier of suppliers and customers. In 2025, the 
Company had approximately 15,000 active 
direct suppliers, of which approximately 200 
provided materials and components used 
in Ericsson’s hardware. The customer base 
is comparatively concentrated: out of more 
than 500 customers, the 10 largest, mainly 
communications service providers, accounted 
for 46% (44%) of net sales.
The global electronics manufacturing 
value chain begins with the extraction of nat-
ural resources used in electronic hardware. 
These materials are refined, traded and man-
ufactured into parts and components that are 
assembled into finished products. Ericsson’s 
regional supply hubs consolidate material 
from component suppliers and distribute it to 
production sites. 
Manufacturing and assembly of com-
munication equipment take place both at 
Ericsson’s own sites and at contracted elec-
tronics manufacturing suppliers, which in 
2025 produced 80% (78%) of the Company’s 
hardware output. The map on the next page

upstream activities include suppliers provid-

Scoping and assessment
The process began by defining the universe 
of relevant ESG matters, drawing on widely 
used reporting frameworks, peer and cus-
tomer benchmarking and methodologies of 
selected ESG rating providers. Topics with no 
clear link to Ericsson’s business or value chain 
were excluded.
The remaining matters were assessed to 
identify actual and potential negative and 
positive impacts, as well as financially mate-
rial risks and opportunities. Input included 
research on environmental impacts of 
Ericsson’s products and solutions, findings 
from human rights due diligence activities, 
existing risk management processes and 
stakeholder engagement insights. Sources 
such as scientific studies, NGO and industry 
reports, ESG risk intelligence tools, supplier 
audits, employee surveys and cases reported 
via the Ericsson Compliance Line were also 
considered.
Negative impacts were evaluated based 
on severity (scale, scope and irremediability) 
and, for potential impacts, the likelihood of 
occurrence. Positive impacts were assessed 
by scale and scope. Downstream impacts 
were considered only when directly linked to 
Ericsson’s products, solutions or technologies. 
Quantitative scoring of scale and scope were 
complemented by qualitative thresholds and 
professional judgment. Impacts assessed as 
high in both scale and scope were generally 
considered material, with irremediability 
guiding decisions in borderline cases.
The assessment of risks and opportunities 
focused primarily on matters where material 
impacts had been identified, supplemented 
by systemic risks such as climate change. 
Financial magnitude and likelihood deter-
mined materiality, and thresholds for both 
were set to align with Ericsson’s Enterprise 
Risk Management (ERM) framework. Risks 
and opportunities were considered material 
when both magnitude and likelihood were 
high, with discretion applied in specific cases.
Alignment with the ERM framework
The alignment with the ERM framework 
ensures consistency between financial 
and non-financial risk considerations. 
Sustainability-­related risks are treated on  
the same basis as other risk categories such 
as strategic risks and are not subject to higher 
or lower prioritization. As a general principle, 
risks not considered material in the ERM pro-
cess required clear justification to be classi-
fied as financially material in the materiality 
assessment. 
Opportunities were evaluated alongside 
risks, applying the same magnitude and 
­likelihood criteria.
Climate-related considerations 
The assessment incorporated results of pre-
vious climate scenario analyses. Ericsson’s 
initial analysis compared a Current Policies 
scenario with a Net Zero 2050 pathway. The 
Current Policies scenario assumes that only 
climate and energy policies implemented or 
announced at the time of the analysis are 
maintained, resulting in continued growth 
in global GHG emissions, a temperature 
increase well above 2 C and rising physical 
climate risks over time. In contrast, the Net 
Zero 2050 scenario assumes immediate and 
coordinated global policy action to achieve 
net zero emissions by 2050, limiting warm-
ing to around 1.5 C, with higher near-term 
transition pressures but substantially lower 
long-term physical climate risks. Short-term 
effects to 2025 and mid-term effects to 
2030 were partly quantified, while long-term 
effects beyond 2030 were assessed qualita­
tively. Location-specific data was used to 
assess physical risks, while transition effects 
were assessed at broader industry or socio-
economic levels. The selected scenarios are 
considered relevant, as they provide two 
contrasting pathways with diverging implica-
tions for Ericsson and the ICT sector, and the 
time horizons align with the first milestone of 
Ericsson’s transition plan. 
The main transition effects under the Net 
Zero 2050 pathway included greater cus-
tomer demand for energy-efficient networks 
and connectivity infrastructure as a result of 
broader societal action to reduce emissions, 
for example through continued automation 
and digitalization. In contrast, the Current 
Policies scenario highlighted rising physical 
hazards for certain component suppliers due 
to more frequent extreme weather events.
In 2025, a supplemental analysis was 
undertaken focusing on physical risks at 
Ericsson’s manufacturing and logistics sites, 
as well as selected key supplier sites. Two sce-
narios, warming of 3 C and 5 C by 2100, were 
examined across short-term (to 2030), mid-
term (to 2060) and long-term (beyond 2060) 
horizons. The analysis indicated a substantial 
increase in physical risks after 2060 under 
both scenarios, with greater exposure in the 
5 C pathway. Given Ericsson’s ­geographically 
diversified footprint, individual sites are 
exposed to varying degrees of physical cli-
mate risks also over shorter to medium-term 
time horizons. However, when assessed on a 
consolidated basis, these risks did not meet 
the threshold for financial materiality applied 
in the materiality assessment, also consid-
ering the inherent uncertainty in predicting 
the likelihood and severity of climate-related 
events.
The outcomes and conclusions from the 
scenario analyses performed are inherently 
subject to uncertainty, as they are based 
on assumptions about future conditions 
and developments that may or may not 
occur, or may differ materially from actual 
developments.
Topic-specific screening
In 2025, Ericsson screened key internal sites, 
such as manufacturing, logistics, data centers 
and labs, as well as selected direct supplier 
sites for water- and nature-related impacts. 
Ericsson’s manufacturing sites are assembly-­
based and located in urban or semi-urban 
areas, with no heavy industrial activities, lim-
iting location-specific and pollution-­related 
impacts. Water is sourced from municipal 
systems and not used in manufacturing 
processes, resulting in limited water-related 
impacts.
The analysis showed that while some sites 
are located near biodiversity-sensitive areas 
or in regions with higher water stress, none 
of these exposures was significant enough to 
be classified as material impacts or risks at a 
consolidated level.
Ericsson did not undertake significant 
construction of new sites during the reporting 
period. As a result, resource use and circularity 
impacts arise primarily from the manufactur-
ing and sale of mobile network equipment, 
rather than from fixed assets.
For business conduct matters, Ericsson 
considered the specific risk profile of the tele-
communications sector, which faces elevated 
exposure due to its technical complexity, 
reliance on evolving geopolitical develop-
ments and close interaction with both public 
and private actors. Inputs were drawn from 
Ericsson’s compliance risk assessments, 
monitoring of geopolitical developments and 
cases reported through the Compliance Line.
Stakeholder validation and governance 
Preliminary results were reviewed by inter-
nal subject matter experts and business 
representatives to validate conclusions and 
ensure awareness of material matters across 
the organization. A cross-functional group 
of senior leaders reviewed the assessment 
results. 
To supplement the internal validation,  
a not-for-profit organization with expertise 
in human rights reviewed the human- and 
labor-rights impacts, providing an external 
perspective on issues likely to be relevant for 
workers and communities. This review did 
not identify any gaps or issues that required 
changes to the assessment. Beyond this, no

until the close of the Annual General Meeting 
2026. Ten are non-executive directors, and 
the President and CEO serves as the sole 
executive director. In addition, under ­Swedish

employee representatives and three deputy 
employee representatives.
The Board as a whole has access to 
the information shared with its subcom-
mittees on sustainability-related matters,

­Sustainability Statement as part of the

addresses access to grievance mechanisms

withhold, or reclaim such compensation in 
line with its internal sanction process and 
applicable legal requirements. 
The Remuneration Committee reviews 
and prepares for resolution by the Board 
­proposals to the Annual General Meeting on 
the long-term variable compensation pro-
gram and similar equity arrangements. The 
Remuneration Committee also approves 
target levels of short-term variable compen-
sation for the Executive Team, excluding the 
President and CEO. 
Non-executive members of the Board  
of Directors do not receive variable or perfor-
mance-based compensation.
Further details on Ericsson’s remuneration 
practices are provided in the Remuneration 
Report.
Risk management and internal control 
over sustainability reporting
Ericsson applies a structured risk manage-
ment approach to its sustainability reporting 
process. Reporting risks across the Sustain-
ability Statement are assessed using a frame-
work that considers information complexity, 
data source reliability, value-chain depen-
dencies, stakeholder sensitivity and process 
maturity.
Areas with elevated reporting risk typically 
include disclosures based on multiple data 
systems or external information, as well as 
those requiring complex estimations. These 
risks are mitigated through documented 
methodologies, gradual system integration, 
automated consolidation where possible  
and engagement with key data providers  
to support accuracy and consistency.
Reporting and accounting policies are 
in place for all key sustainability areas. 
­Dedicated reporting software now supports 
most numerical disclosures through stan-
dardized data collection and automated 
consolidation, with remaining metrics to be 
integrated going forward. Internal controls 
include four-eye reviews, analytical proce-
dures to detect deviations and complete-
ness checks prior to consolidation. Work to 
establish a formalized control framework for 
sustainability disclosures began in 2025, with 
key controls defined for selected metrics with 
heightened risks. Broader implementation 
will follow as the framework develops. As 
the framework matures, periodic reporting of 
control-related findings will be introduced.
The Audit and Compliance Committee is 
regularly informed of progress in strength-
ening internal control over sustainability 
reporting.

E   Climate change
Mobile networks form part of the critical infra-
structure that enables digital solutions across 
the economy. Applications such as smart 
grids, building management systems, logis-
tics optimization and industrial automation 
depend on reliable connectivity and can sup-
port efficiency improvements and reduced 
energy intensity across multiple sectors. 
While Ericsson does not quantify avoided 
emissions from such applications, its technol-
ogy plays an enabling role in customers’ and 
societies’ efforts to improve energy efficiency 
and resource use. This actual positive impact 
is current and expected to increase over 
the medium to long term as digitalization 
expands. 
At the same time, activities within Ericsson 
and its value chain give rise to greenhouse 
gas (GHG) emissions. Most emissions occur 
downstream during the use phase of sold 
products while operating mobile networks. 
A smaller share arises from upstream activi-
ties, including material extraction, manufac-
turing and transport of network equipment. 
Emissions from Ericsson’s own operations 
are limited compared with the overall value 
chain but remain a focus area, as they are 
within the Company’s direct control. These 
emissions constitute actual negative impacts 
that are currently occurring but are expected 
to decline over the medium to long term. As 
customers use more renewable electricity 
and the share of renewables in national grids 
increases, emissions from operating ­networks 
are expected to decrease. Over time, this 
shift is expected to result in emissions from 
upstream activities representing a larger 
share of total emissions.
Ericsson’s Net Zero target validated by the 
Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), along 
with targets to reduce the energy consumption 
of typical radio base station sites and lower 
the embodied carbon emissions of products, 
provides the strategic direction for addressing 
these impacts across the value chain.
The energy performance of Ericsson’s 
networks is a material transition risk and 
a material opportunity, which is current 
and expected to persist over the medium 
to long term. Energy is a major cost driver 
for communications service providers and 
­therefore a key factor in purchasing decisions. 
Continued investment in R&D to improve 
energy performance can enhance the portfo-
lio’s competitiveness and support demand. If 
­sufficient investments are not made or do not 
result in adequate improvements, demand 
for Ericsson’s solutions could be adversely 
affected. 
Resilience of business model  
to effects of climate change
Ericsson has conducted climate scenario 
analyses, described on page 99, to assess 
effects on its business model and its resilience 
under different climate pathways. Demand 
for mobile networks and connectivity is not 
primarily driven by climate change mitigation 
or adaptation activities, which means that 
the business model and commercial offering 
remain broadly compatible with a range of 
climate scenarios. 
The relevance of improved network energy 
performance varies across scenarios. In path-
ways where the global economy rapidly elec-
trifies and emissions decrease, higher energy 
costs for customers could further increase 
demand for more energy-efficient networks.
Physical risks, such as those linked 
to extreme weather events, could affect 
Ericsson’s global supply and manufactur-
ing value chain. These risks are not unique 
to Ericsson but are common to companies 
with complex global supply chains. Within 
the time horizons applied in the materiality 
assessment, no material physical risks were 
identified.
Policies
Ericsson’s Sustainability Policy sets out the 
Company’s principles on environmental 
­sustainability. The policy requires Ericsson  
to reduce the negative environmental impact 
of its own operations, take a precautionary 
approach to environmental challenges and 
advocate for the use of ICT-solutions to miti-
gate and adapt to climate change. 
The Code of Conduct for Business ­Partners 
requires Ericsson’s suppliers and other busi-
ness partners to develop and implement 
plans and targets to reduce their GHG emis-
sions. Business partners must adopt and pub-
licly disclose their targets and annual progress 
for reducing emissions in alignment with the 
science-based 1.5 C ambition. Ericsson has 
additional environmental requirements for 
suppliers of hardware components or prod-
ucts, construction work, supply services, field 
maintenance and network rollout operations, 
as well as those with high environmental 
risks. These requirements state that if energy 
consumption or GHG emissions are identified 
as significant environmental aspects, the sup-
plier must calculate its carbon footprint, using 
the GHG Protocol for its Scope 1, Scope 2 and, 
as applicable, for its Scope 3 emissions. For 
further information regarding policies, includ-
ing information about Ericsson’s Sustainability 
Policy applicable to its own operations, see 
the section 
 General disclosures. 
Transition plan for climate  
change mitigation
Ericsson has an SBTi validated 1.5 C aligned 
target to reach Net Zero value-chain emis-
sions by 2040. The near-term target is a 50% 
reduction of total value-chain emissions by 
2030, compared with a 2020 baseline.
Scope 1 direct emissions
Ericsson plans to reduce Scope 1 ­emissions 
mainly by transitioning to a smaller, low-­
emission vehicle fleet and expanding fleet 
management systems to optimize vehicle 
use. Additional reductions are expected from 
relocating operations to facilities with district 
heating, replacing gas boilers with electric 
systems where feasible, and by using refrig-
erants with lower global warming potential 
while minimizing their overall use.
The planned measures are expected to 
reduce annual Scope 1 GHG emissions by 
approximately 37,000 metric tons, or 84%, 
by 2030. 
Scope 2 indirect emissions
Ericsson plans to continue sourcing renew-
able electricity for its facilities and to collabo­
rate with facility management partners to 
further improve energy efficiency.
These measures are expected to reduce 
annual Scope 2 GHG emissions by approxi-
mately 70,000 metric tons, or 94%, by 2030.

Scope 3 upstream, transportation  
and product end-of-life emissions
Most planned upstream emission reductions 
focus on lowering embodied carbon emissions 
in Ericsson’s product portfolio. Key measures 
include lightweight product design, alterna-
tive material choices, increased supplier use 
of renewable energy and improved transport 
efficiency. Supplier engagement will prior-
itize those contributing most to Ericsson’s 
supply-chain emissions, such as aluminum 
die-casting, and the manufacturing of printed 
circuit boards and integrated circuits.
Business travel emissions are expected to 
increase from the 2020 baseline, which was 
affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, but are 
not expected to exceed 50% of pre-pandemic 
levels. 
The planned measures are expected to 
contribute to a net reduction of annual Scope 
3 upstream, transportation and product end-
of-life GHG emissions by approximately 1.3 
million metric tons, or 50%, by 2030.
Scope 3 downstream emissions from the 
use of sold products
Ericsson relies on three main levers to reduce 
indirect downstream emissions from the use 
of its products. The size of these levers has 
been estimated based on projected sales and 
forecasted energy consumption of hardware 
and software.
The first and most significant lever within 
Ericsson’s direct control is improving the 
energy performance of hardware, software 
and service solutions. A key progress ­indicator 
is the target to reduce the average energy 
consumption of typical radio base station 
sites. Ericsson is also providing guidance to 
customers on planning, building and operat-
ing energy-optimized networks. This lever is 
expected to reduce annual GHG emissions 
by approximately 8.6 million metric tons by 
2030.
The second lever involves supporting 
­customers’ transition to renewable electricity. 
While Ericsson cannot directly influence elec-
tricity purchasing decisions, the Company 
facilitates this shift by enabling integration of 
on-site renewable solutions, such as solar and 
wind power, at base station sites. Ericsson’s 
transition plan assumes a conservative esti-
mate of approximately 50% renewable elec-
tricity use by customers in 2030, which is lower 
than projections from the Global System for 
Mobile Communications Association (GSMA). 
This lever is expected to reduce annual emis-
sions by approximately 5.1 million metric tons.
The third lever is the expected growth of 
fossil-­free energy in national electricity grids 
powering mobile networks. This depends on 
external factors, including national energy 
policies, and is therefore subject to high uncer-
tainty. Depending on the scenario, this lever 
could contribute to annual emission reductions 
ranging from zero to 6.3 million metric tons. 
Together, these levers are expected to con-
tribute to a net reduction of annual Scope 3 
downstream GHG emissions from the use  
of sold products by between 13.7 and 20.0 
million metric tons, or 50% to 73%, by 2030.
Financial resources allocated  
to the transition plan 
Climate-related actions and initiatives are 
embedded in Ericsson’s ongoing operations 
and business planning. Emission-reduction 
measures within own operations do not 
currently incur material capital or operating 
expenditures warranting separate disclosure. 
The largest emission source, downstream 
emissions from the use of sold products, 
is addressed primarily through improved 
­product energy performance driven by R&D 
activities and through customer actions such 
as the use of renewable electricity.
Part of Ericsson’s R&D investments to 
enhance the energy performance of exist-
ing and future products is financed through 
green bonds. In 2023, Ericsson issued its 
inaugural EUR 500 million green bond under 
its Green Financing Framework, and by the 
end of 2024 all proceeds had been allocated 
to hardware and software R&D to support 
Ericsson’s goal to reduce the energy con-
sumption of typical radio base station sites. 
Total R&D expenditure is disclosed on page 
14 of the Board of Directors’ Report.
The Company’s activities are not, to any 
significant extent, covered by the delegated 
regulations on climate change mitigation or 
adaptation under the EU taxonomy. Accord-
ingly, no material investments are currently 
planned to align with the taxonomy criteria 
for these environmental objectives.
Locked-in emissions
Cumulative locked-in GHG emissions from 
Ericsson’s own operations are not considered 
material, as Ericsson does not operate any 
emission-intensive assets. Locked-in emissions 
from the use phase of sold products depend 
on the electricity required to power customer 
networks, and therefore on customers’ energy 
sourcing choices. 
Alignment with EU Paris-­aligned 
­benchmarks
Based on the exclusion criteria defined under 
the relevant regulation, Ericsson has assessed 
that it is not excluded from the EU Paris-­aligned 
benchmarks.
Governance of the transition plan
The transition plan was reviewed and 
adopted by a group of senior leaders repre-
senting the business segments Networks and 
Cloud Software and Services, as well as group 
functions including sourcing, finance, real 
estate and sustainability. It was subsequently 
presented to the Executive Team members 
leading these units. The plan and its under-
lying assumptions will be reviewed regularly 
and updated as needed to reflect significant 
business changes. 
The Company does not expect actions 
related to its Net Zero transition to result 
in material negative impacts on its own 
workforce.
Targets
Ericsson has set both near-term and long-
term targets for reducing its emissions. Both 
the targets and the baseline are group-wide 
and have been validated by the SBTi as 1.5 C

GHG removals and carbon credits
No carbon credits were purchased during 
2025. Ericsson plans to use carbon removal 
technologies to neutralize the unavoidable 
part of value-chain emissions to reach its 
2040 Net Zero targets.
Internal carbon pricing
Ericsson currently does not apply an internal 
carbon price that results in internal transfer of 
funds or that is used when preparing ﬁnancial 
statements.
GHG accounting methodology
Emissions are reported in accordance with 
the GHG Protocol, using the same consolida­
tion approach as for the ﬁnancial statements. 
If Ericsson were to gain operational control 
over a non-consolidated entity or asset, 
related Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions would 
be included based on operational control 
rather than equity share. No such arrange­
ments existed during the reporting year, and 
operational boundaries remained unchanged 
from the previous period.
Emission calculations are based on the 
latest available data at the cut-off date, sup­
plemented with extrapolated estimates for 
periods without measured data. Emissions 
are reported in CO2e and include carbon 
dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide 
(N2O), hydroﬂuorocarbons (HFCs), perﬂuo­
rochemicals (PFCs), sulfur hexaﬂuoride (SF6) 
and nitrogen triﬂuoride (NF3). The most sig­
niﬁcant emission factors applied are listed in 
Appendix 4.
Scope 1 
Consumed volumes of fuels and refrigerants 
are multiplied by applicable emission factors 
to derive emissions. Fuel consumption in 
the service-vehicle ﬂeet is calculated using 
a combination of telematics data and inter­
nal estimates. For leased vehicles lacking 
telematics, consumption is estimated from 
contracted annual mileage and internal 
assessments of driven distances. 
Scope 2
Purchased-energy volumes are converted 
to emissions using country-speciﬁc average 
factors for location-based calculations. For 
market-based emissions, factors are derived 
from the residual energy mix and purchased 
renewable-energy instruments. Further 
details are provided in the subsection Energy 
consumption and mix in own operations.
Scope 3
Emission factors for the categories Capital 
goods, Fuel- and energy-related activities, 
Waste generated in operations, and End-
of-life treatment of sold products are largely 
based on internal studies and Ericsson’s 
life-cycle assessment of product carbon foot­
prints, multiplied by relevant activity metrics 
to estimate annual emissions.
Emissions in the Purchased goods and 
 services category are estimated using cradle-
to-gate emissions calculated per product, 
based on material composition and supplier- 
speciﬁc emission factors from primary and 
secondary data sources. Per-unit cradle-to-
gate emissions are multiplied by the number 
of delivered units. This category also includes 
emissions from externally purchased 
cloud-storage and processing capacity.
Upstream transportation emissions are 
estimated using a mix of spend-based data 
and calculations derived from shipment 
weights and distances paid for by Ericsson. 
Business travel emissions are calculated 
primarily from ﬂight route, distance and 
ticket-class data, with hotel nights estimated 
from travel spend. Employee commuting 
emissions are based on surveys of employees’ 
commuting and teleworking habits.
Lifetime product emissions in the Use of 
sold products category are estimated and 
reported in full in the year the products are 
sold, assuming an average product lifetime of 
10 years. Life-cycle grid-emission factors for 
the use phase are estimated from the current 
energy mix of markets served, or from cus­
tomer-speciﬁc energy-mix data when publicly 
available. Future changes in grid factors or 
customer energy mixes are not reﬂected.
Downstream transportation emissions are 
mainly calculated from shipment weights and 
distances where transport is paid for by the 
customer. 
The remaining Scope 3 categories have 
been assessed as not material and are there­
fore not reported.
The reported ﬁgures are subject to uncer­
tainty due to data limitations and should be 
regarded as estimates rather than precise 
values. The accompanying table summarizes

Most electronic components contain small 
amounts of substances of concern, and in 
some cases substances of very high concern. 
These substances are used during manu-
facturing and are therefore embedded in the 
finished products that Ericsson sells. If not 
properly managed or disposed of at end-of-
life, these substances can leak into the envi-
ronment and harm ecosystems and human 
health.
These are potential negative impacts of a 
systemic nature, occurring mainly upstream 
in Ericsson’s value chain, where such sub-
stances are used in component manufactur-
ing, and downstream when products are not 
properly recycled. Ericsson’s own operations 
primarily involve the assembly of components 
and therefore do not involve the addition of 
significant volumes of these substances. The 
exposure to these impacts is current, but their 
magnitude is expected to decline over the 
medium to long term, assuming Ericsson con-
tinues to phase out some of these substances 
from its products. 
While not identified as material risks in the 
materiality assessment, regulatory develop-
ments, such as proposals to restrict the use 
of PFAS1) in the European Union, represent 
emerging issues that Ericsson monitors and 
integrates into its strategy from a precau-
tionary perspective. Depending on the final 
requirements, such developments could in 
the long term lead to higher compliance costs, 
additional research and development needs 
or constraints in the availability of alternative 
materials.
Policies 
In addition to Ericsson’s Code of Conduct for 
Business Partners, suppliers with significant 
environmental impact such as manufacturing 
service providers, shipping and logistics com-
panies and network rollout partners, must 
meet additional environmental requirements. 
These include compliance with Ericsson’s 
Lists of Banned and Restricted Substances, 
which identify substances that are restricted 
for use in products or in the production of pur-
chased components. This requirement also 
applies to substances used in batteries and 
packaging. 
The structure and classification of sub-
stances follow the Material Declaration for 
Products of and for the Electrotechnical 
Industry standard, IEC 62474, and include 
additional substances defined by Ericsson. 
Banned and restricted substances may not be 
intentionally added in specified applications, 
and substitution of substances under obser-
vation is recommended as a precautionary 
measure. Further information about the Code 
of Conduct for Business Partners is included 
in the section 
 General disclosures. 
Management actions 
Material declarations
To monitor substances in purchased com-
ponents and equipment, Ericsson collects 
material declarations from suppliers. Upon 
request, suppliers must declare the full mate-
rial content, including substances on the 
REACH2) candidate list and certain raw mate-
rials defined in the EU Critical Raw Materials 
List. A SCIP3) reporting process is in place to 
meet reporting requirements of the EU Waste 
Framework Directive. Ericsson collaborates 
with hardware suppliers and encourages 
proactive substitution of substances under 
observation where feasible.
Management of electronic waste
To meet extended producer responsibilities 
for electrical and electronic equipment, 
Ericsson offers collection of end-of-life prod-
ucts to its customers through its e-Waste 
Management Program. The program helps 
reduce the risk of hazardous substances in 
products being disposed of in ways that could 
cause pollution. Further information is pro-
vided in the section 
 Resource use and 
­circular economy. 
Environmental Management System
Ericsson’s environmental management 
system is certified to the ISO 14001:2015 
standard and covers management, research, 
product management, development, supply, 
sales, installation and maintenance of hard-
ware, software, services and solutions for 
ICT. It is integrated into the Ericsson Group 
Management System and includes processes 
for audits, assessments and management 
reviews. Environmental regulations are reg-
ularly monitored at country level to support 
local compliance. 
An environmental risk management 
framework is in place, aligned with Ericsson’s 
overall ERM framework. Employees shall 
report environmental incidents through the 
Company’s incident reporting system, and 
suppliers are required to do the same as 
set out in the Code of Conduct for Business 
Partners. 
Regulatory monitoring
In 2025, Ericsson continued to monitor 
­substance-related regulatory developments, 
such as PFAS, in the markets where it oper-
ates to assess potential implications for its 
business and the telecommunications sector.
Targets
Ericsson has not set targets for its ­material 
pollution-related impacts but continues 
to assess whether target setting would be 
appropriate as part of its management 
approach. The effectiveness of Ericsson’s 
policies and actions in these areas is, in part, 
monitored through the collection of material 
declarations from its suppliers.
Emissions to air from own ­operations 
Although not linked to any material impacts, 
risks or opportunities, emissions of air pollut-
ants from Ericsson’s operations are disclosed 
in Appendix 5, as this information is frequently 
requested by external stakeholders. These 
emissions mainly arise from fossil fuel com-
bustion in the service vehicle fleet and from 
local heating at facilities. 
Most of Ericsson’s own manufacturing 
sites are not within the scope of regulations 
related to air pollutants, such as the European 
Union’s Emissions Trading Scheme, the 
Industrial Emissions Directive or the European 
Pollutant Release and Transfer Register. 
Ericsson complies with all applicable local 
regulations on the control and monitoring of 
emissions to air.

value chain, primarily in semiconductor man-

Semiconductor production requires very

at different stages, with consequences for 
both water availability and quality in affected 
areas. The impact is linked to Ericsson’s busi-

ers of semiconductors and raw materials used 
in network equipment.
No material water-related impacts have 
been identified in Ericsson’s own operations 
or downstream value chain. Water use in 
Ericsson’s facilities is limited to sanitary

Water shortages in regions where suppli-
ers are located could, over time, affect the 
availability of critical inputs such as semicon-
ductors or minerals. Several regions where 
suppliers operate, including Southeast Asia, 
are projected to face high water stress in the 
medium to long term. These are not currently 
material risks for Ericsson, but are considered 
emerging matters that the Company monitors 
as part of its supply-chain management and 
long-term strategy.

E   Resource use and circular economy
As part of its materiality assessment, Ericsson 
evaluated its impacts on biodiversity and 
ecosystems. The key drivers of biodiversity 
loss and ecosystem degradation linked to 
Ericsson’s direct and indirect activities are 
climate change, use of natural resources 
and pollution. These impacts, along with 
Ericsson’s approach to managing them, are 
addressed in other sections of the Sustain-
ability Statement.
Other drivers, such as land- and sea- use 
change, land degradation, desertification, 
and invasive species, were not identified as 
material in Ericsson’s value chain. 
Ericsson’s own facilities are located in 
urban or semi-urban areas, with limited 
impact on land use and surrounding eco-
systems. The Company supports customers 
in the installation of telecommunication 
networks and network sites. When planning 
these installations, standard procedures are 
applied to minimize environmental impacts, 
including site location planning to reduce 
land-use effects.
Ericsson addresses biodiversity-related 
impacts primarily through actions to mitigate 
climate change, reduce pollution and transition 
to a more circular business model. Biodiversity 
and ecosystems are therefore not currently 
managed or reported on as a standalone topic.
Resource inflows and outflows
Producing hardware for mobile networks 
requires metals and minerals such as iron, 
aluminum, copper and, even though in 
smaller volumes, rare earth elements and 
other raw materials. Extracting and process-
ing these finite resources causes negative 
environmental impacts and contributes to 
the scarcity and depletion of global resources. 
These actual negative impacts are current 
and expected to persist over the medium to 
long term. They are concentrated upstream 
in the value chain, where mining and refining 
take place. 
Although many metals like aluminum 
and copper are widely recycled, rare earth 
elements and some other raw materials 
have low recycling rates and limited substi-
tutes, which sustains the need for primary 
extraction. Ericsson does not process raw 
materials in its own operations and mainly 
assembles components, but can influence 
material efficiency, recyclability, product life-
time and the use of recycled inputs through 
product design. Strengthening resource cir-
cularity also brings climate benefits because 
reduced reliance on primary materials lowers 
related upstream emissions.
Resource inflows and outflows are not 
considered a financially material risk for 
Ericsson today, based on the latest materi-
ality assessment. However, the long-term 
availability of certain metals and minerals 
remains important to monitor, since global 
demand may affect sourcing conditions and 
supply-chain resilience. Ongoing oversight of 
these dependencies supports efforts to ease 
pressure on finite resources and helps main-
tain stable access to materials for electronic 
manufacturing.
Waste
Electronic waste (e-waste) is one of the fast-
est-growing waste streams globally, and net-
work hardware is part of this trend. Inefficient 
production processes combined with limited 
collection of end-of-life equipment contribute 
to negative environmental impacts, including 
risks of improper treatment and pollution.
These actual negative impacts are current 
and expected to persist over the medium to 
long term. They occur both upstream and 
downstream in the value chain. Upstream, 
manufacturing processes generate waste 
during component production. Downstream, 
recovery and treatment of used equipment 
pose challenges. Ericsson’s take-back rates 
for network hardware remain low, partly 
because ownership lies with customers and 
products often retain resale value. While 
resale and second-hand markets can extend 
equipment lifetime, they may reduce trace-
ability and limit the likelihood of proper recy-
cling. As a result, some equipment is assumed 
to be recycled under substandard conditions. 
In its own operations, Ericsson generates 
relatively little waste, though unsold and 
scrapped inventory constitutes a notable 
internal waste stream, albeit smaller in scale 
than customer-owned end-of-life equipment.
E-waste-related risks are currently not 
considered financially material for Ericsson. 
Nevertheless, with global e-waste volumes 
projected to rise further, this remains an 
important issue to monitor. Addressing 
e-waste through improved collection and 
treatment practices supports responsible 
resource management, reduces environmental 
pressures and contributes to the long-term 
resilience of the electronics value chain.
Policies
Ericsson’s Sustainability Policy sets out  
the Company’s principles on environmental 
sustainability. The policy requires Ericsson 
to provide product take-back services to its 
customers as part of its extended producer 
responsibility, and to support them in the 
end-of-life management of products and 
solutions. 
In addition to the Code of Conduct for 
­Business Partners, suppliers with significant 
environmental impact such as manufacturing 
service providers, shipping and logistics com-
panies and network rollout partners must 
meet additional environmental requirements. 
These suppliers are expected to apply a system­
atic approach to identify, manage, reduce and 
responsibly dispose of or recycle non-hazard-
ous solid waste. They are also expected to con-
serve natural resources, including water, fossil 
fuels, minerals and virgin forest products, 
through measures such as process modifica-
tions, material substitution, reuse, conservation 
and recycling, where feasible.

Management actions
Product design principles 
Ericsson applies the Design for Environment 
principles throughout its product design pro-
cesses. Key requirements include material 
marking, ease of dismantling and disassembly 
to support maintenance and recycling, and 
durability for long product life as part of quality 
management. Banned and restricted sub-
stances lists and material declaration require-
ments, described in the section 
 Pollution, 
guide material selection to support regulatory 
compliance and improve recyclability.
Products returned through the e-Waste 
Management Program described below have 
historically shown high recyclability, averaging 
above 90% in recent years. Ericsson also works 
to reduce product weight and size and is 
assessing more sustainable material options 
in line with its Net Zero target, supporting 
more efficient resource use and contributing 
to circularity across the product life cycle. 
Refurbish, reuse and repair
Ericsson applies a structured approach to 
refurbishment and reuse within its Support 
Services portfolio. Shared warehouses and 
spare-parts solutions help limit the need for 
new production, and automated hardware 
fault analysis reduces unnecessary replace-
ments. Ericsson also provides repair services 
and enables the reuse of returned equipment, 
which complements new product sales and 
supports circularity across the product life cycle.
Management of e-waste
Ericsson operates a global e-Waste Manage-
ment Program in collaboration with third-party 
recyclers that are required to meet stringent 
environmental requirements. Through this 
program, customer-owned products at the 
end-of-life stage can be collected and recycled 
to help minimize environmental impact.  
A limited number of subsidiaries provide take-
back services through collective take-back 
schemes, reflecting the nature of their product 
portfolios. As equipment typically remains the 
property of customers, take-back volumes 
depend on customer use of these programs. 
Waste from own operations
Ericsson primarily assembles parts and 
components from suppliers and therefore 
gener­ates relatively little material waste, 
mainly office waste and residuals from pro-
duction and packaging. During the year, the 
Company carried out targeted work to better 
quantify unsold inventory that is scrapped, 
with the aim of reducing these volumes over 
time. Ericsson also continued its programs 
that focus on waste reduction and improved 
waste handling in offices and warehouses. 
Critical minerals 
Ericsson manages risks related to critical min-
erals, including rare earth elements, as part of 
its general sourcing processes to ensure con-
tinuity of supply and access to key production 
inputs. Because Ericsson purchases compo-
nents and finished products rather than raw 
materials directly, its exposure to these mate-
rials is indirect and primarily occurs through 
its supply chain. 
To maintain supply continuity, suppliers 
are segmented by business criticality based 
on spend, risk, dependency and strategic 
importance. Ericsson manages disruption 
risks through multiple sourcing options, stra-
tegic buffer stocks and real-time monitoring 
of disruptive events. This monitoring helps 
identify suppliers affected by man-made or 
natural disruptions and supports the imple-
mentation of mitigation measures. It may 
also draw on supplier business continuity 
plans to provide greater detail into potential 
vulnerabilities. 
Targets
Ericsson has not set targets for its material 
resource use and circularity-related impacts 
but continues to assess whether target setting 
would be appropriate as part of its manage-
ment approach. The effectiveness of related 
policies and actions is, in part, monitored 
through its e-waste-related key performance 
indicators (KPIs) as disclosed on the next page.
Resource inflows
Building on its indirect exposure to raw mate-
rials through the supply chain, Ericsson is 
working to improve visibility into the material 
composition of purchased products and com-
ponents. At present, the Company has limited 
supplier-specific data on the share of second-
ary raw materials incorporated into these 
inputs.
Network equipment consists primarily of 
metals, and an analysis of the Bills of Materials 
for key products indicates that a typical radio 
is composed of approximately 58% aluminum, 
10% copper, 8% iron or steel, 4% rubber and 
3% silicon. The remaining share is made up  
of other compounds, including limited use of 
polymers such as polycarbonates (plastics), 
and less than 1% rare earth elements. Several 
of these materials are listed by the EU as 
­critical raw materials. 
In 2025, the total weight of materials 
used in Ericsson’s network equipment was 
approximately 103,000 metric tons, of which 
an estimated 3,000 metric tons (3%) were 
secondary materials, including recycled or 
reused components1). The estimate is derived 
from data provided by key suppliers and 
from global average recycling rates for the 
materials most frequently used in Ericsson’s 
highest-­volume products. As a result, the 
quality and the granularity of the data remain 
limited, and further improvements to the 
measurement methodology are planned. 
Resource outflows
Products and materials 
Primary resource outflows from Ericsson’s 
production and outsourced manufacturing 
consist of network hardware, including radios, 
antennas, basebands, power modules, rout-
ers and modems, as well as site materials 
such as cables and batteries and associated 
packaging. All products designed by Ericsson 
follow generic product requirements and the 
Design for Environment principles, including 
considerations for repairability, as described 
above.
There is no established industry benchmark 
for the average expected durability of network 
equipment, which means that comparisons 
between Ericsson’s hardware and that of 
peers are not possible. Ericsson’s network hard­
ware is also not covered by any reparability 
rating system, as such schemes are generally 
designed for consumer electronics.
Ericsson’s network equipment mainly 
consists of metals that are widely recyclable. 
Based on data from recycling of its own prod-
ucts, it is estimated that 96% of the materials 
are recyclable2).
Waste
Ericsson’s material waste streams are the 
end-of-life treatment of customer-owned 
network equipment and the scrapping of 
unsold inventory of similar products. Both 
streams consist primarily of electronic waste 
that contains the materials listed under the 
subsection Resource inflows above.

The EU taxonomy establishes a common 
framework to identify which economic activi-
ties can be considered environmentally sus-
tainable. Ericsson has assessed its economic 
activities against the taxonomy to determine 
which are eligible and aligned under the 
­Climate and Environmental Delegated 
Regulations.
Assessment approach 
Identifying the economic activities relevant 
for Ericsson has required interpretation of 
the taxonomy and the related Delegated 
­Regulations. Ericsson’s interpretation is that, 
for an economic activity to be considered 
­taxonomy eligible, it must meet all three of 
the following criteria:
	
– Generate, or be aimed at generating, 
external turnover,
	
– match the description of an activity listed 
in one of the annexes to the Climate or 
Environmental Delegated Regulation and
	
– have practically applicable technical 
screening criteria associated with it.
Based on this interpretation, turnover, capital 
expenditure (Capex) and operational expen-
diture (Opex) from activities meeting these 
criteria have been included as taxonomy eligi-
ble in the KPIs presented on the next page.  
In addition, certain individually eligible expen-
ditures are included as taxonomy eligible, as 
described below.
As of 2025, Ericsson applies the recently 
introduced materiality thresholds in the tax-
onomy, under which economic activities that 
individually and in aggregate represent no 
more than 10% of turnover, Capex or Opex 
are not disclosed as separate items. These 
non-material activities are listed in a footnote 
to the summary table on the next page.
It should be noted that only a few activities 
in the ICT sector are included in the Climate 
Delegated Regulation. While the European 
Commission has indicated that additional 
activities may be considered in the future, 
most of Ericsson’s commercial offering, 
including mobile networks, is currently not 
covered by activities listed as eligible under 
the Climate Delegated Regulation.
Climate Delegated Regulation
No economic activities that qualify under  
the Climate Delegated Regulation generated 
material turnover, Capex or Opex during the 
reporting year. 
Environmental Delegated Regulation
Manufacture of electrical and electronic 
equipment (CE 1.2)
Ericsson sells electronic equipment as part  
of its network solutions, including radios, 
antennas, basebands, power modules, routers, 
modems and site materials such as cables and 
batteries. The equipment is manufactured 
both at Ericsson’s own sites and by third-party 
electronics manufacturers.
The technical screening criteria for assess-
ing whether this activity makes a substantial 
contribution have been reviewed. The assess-
ment is that these criteria were primarily 
developed for consumer electronics and are 
therefore often not directly applicable to net-
work products. As is common for industrial 
equipment manufacturers, detailed informa-
tion on how network products can be repaired 
or dismantled is not publicly disclosed, as 
doing so could create significant competitive 
disadvantages. In addition, the products do 
not fully comply with all substance require-
ments specified in the criteria. However, the 
criteria related to extended producer respon-
sibility for electrical and electronic equipment 
and batteries are assessed as being met.
Work is ongoing to assess whether this 
activity meets the Do No Significant Harm 
(DNSH) criteria under the EU taxonomy. The 
assessment includes evaluation of impacts 
by primary manufacturing facilities on water 
resources, nature and biodiversity, and expo-
sure to location-specific climate-related 
hazards. As this work is ongoing, it is not yet 
possible to conclude whether all DNSH criteria 
are fully met.
Most DNSH criteria related to pollution 
prevention and control are met. However, the 
general DNSH criteria are not yet fully met, as 
all products currently contain lead. The activ-
ity is assessed as meeting the DNSH criteria 
for climate change mitigation. The criteria 
related to energy-efficiency ratings apply only 
to consumer electronics and are therefore not 
applicable to these products.
Individually eligible expenditures
Material expenditures related to economic 
activities other than those described above 
may be included as individually eligible Capex 
and Opex, provided that the activity is listed in 
either the Climate or Environmental Delegated 
Regulation and that the supplier’s economic 
activity is taxonomy eligible and, where 
­applicable, taxonomy aligned.
Ericsson includes Acquisition and owner­
ship of buildings (CCM 7.7) as individually 
eligible Capex and Opex. As assessing align-
ment for these activities requires detailed 
information on suppliers’ own taxonomy 
alignment, Ericsson is currently not able to 
determine to what extent identified individ-
ually eligible Capex and Opex can also be 
­considered taxonomy aligned.
Certain additional expenditures related 
to activities listed in the Climate Delegated 
Regulation are included within non-material 
activities, as presented in the footnote to the 
summary table on the next page.

Equal treatment and opportunities for all
Ericsson has identified an actual positive 
impact related to the continuous upskilling 
and reskilling of its workforce in critical skills 
such as AI, cloud-native technologies, security, 
leadership, business development, ethics as 
well as health, safety and well-being. By pro-
viding employees with access to learning and 
development in these areas, Ericsson supports 
their long-term employability, career growth 
and professional development. At the same 
time, strengthening these capabilities within 
the workforce enables Ericsson to maintain 
its technology leadership in mobile networks, 
where these skills are increasingly important. 
Providing employees with opportunities to 
build the right skills is critical not only for 
developing innovative solutions, but also  
for effectively bringing them to market and 
meeting customer needs. This alignment of 
employee development with business priori-
ties contributes to a workforce that is better 
prepared for industry transformations while 
supporting Ericsson’s ability to deliver competi­
tive, high-quality solutions to its customers 
and partners. This impact is current and 
expected to persist over the medium to long 
term.
Alongside these positive impacts, Ericsson 
has identified the disproportionately lower 
representation of women as an actual neg-
ative impact across the information and 
communications technology (ICT) sector 
including within its own workforce. Women 
represent a comparatively smaller part of the 
workforce in technical roles and leadership 
positions, areas that are critical to Ericsson’s 
long-term competitiveness as this narrows 
the range of perspectives applied in innova-
tion and decision-making.
The root causes are structural, stemming 
from educational pipelines with low female 
participation in science, technology, engi-
neering and mathematics (STEM), combined 
with long-standing industry norms. This 
systemic impact is current and expected to 
persist over the medium to long term unless 
addressed. Ericsson is committed to uphold-
ing all applicable anti-discrimination laws 
and regulations, and any initiatives in this 
area are developed in accordance with those 
requirements.
Taken together, these impacts illustrate 
how equal treatment and opportunities for all 
are integral to Ericsson’s workforce approach. 
Supporting employees through continuous 
skill development and use of non-discrimina-
tory performance metrics, while addressing 
barriers to representation, contributes both 
to individual career growth and to Ericsson’s 
ability to attract, develop and retain human 
capital, and is an essential factor for success 
in the ICT sector.
Working conditions
Substandard working conditions
Ericsson has employees in more than 100 
countries and operates its own manufacturing 
and logistics sites across Europe, Asia and the 
Americas, which connects the Company to 
potential negative impacts on working condi-
tions across its value chain. These issues are 
systemic in nature and are typically more 
prevalent upstream in the electronics manu-
facturing supply chain. Ericsson’s own expo-
sure primarily relates to employees in manu-
facturing and logistics roles in higher-risk 
geographies, including parts of Latin America, 
South and Southeast Asia and China. Within 
Ericsson’s own operations in these locations, 
the risk of excessive working hours, inadequate 
pay, insecure employment, harassment, and 
restrictions on freedom of association and 
collective bargaining is assessed as heightened.
Ericsson monitors working conditions 
across its operations worldwide through 
ongoing engagement and due diligence 
activities. The underlying conditions giving 
rise to these impacts are current and expected 
to persist over the medium to long term. 
Work-related accidents and fatalities 
Work-related accidents occur in Ericsson’s 
own operations and, to a greater extent, 
among supplier personnel engaged in net-
work rollout, maintenance and repair, where 
fatalities also have occurred. This actual 
negative impact is current and expected to 
persist over the medium and long term. It is 
concentrated in field operations and supplier 
relationships across multiple regions.
Based on past incident data, fatalities 
have resulted from road traffic accidents,  
falls from heights and electrocution among 
supplier personnel working on network sites. 
Lost workday incidents have mainly arisen 
from similar causes, as well as during assembly, 
disassembly and other field-based technical 
activities. These impacts are linked to 
Ericsson’s business model, which involves 
large-scale network deployment and mainte-
nance carried out both by Ericsson and its 
suppliers. 
Ericsson’s Target Zero goal integrates 
health and safety aspects into the Company’s 
overall strategy, aiming to eliminate fatalities 
and lost workday accidents across Ericsson’s 
own operations and its value chain.
Security of workers in high-risk areas
Ericsson has employees and works with sup-
pliers in regions where conflict, political insta-
bility, civil unrest or organized crime create 
heightened security concerns. In such contexts, 
workers in both Ericsson’s own operations 
and its value chain may face threats to their 
safety and well-being, including assault, 
abduction or other forms of violence.
The exposure to such risks is particularly 
relevant for employees and supplier person-
nel engaged in network rollout and mainte-
nance activities in unstable areas. Ericsson is 
directly exposed through its own employees 
in these geographies and indirectly through 
business relationships with suppliers and 
subcontractors. This potential negative 
impact is current and expected to persist  
over the medium to long term.
Upholding fair and safe working conditions 
is central to Ericsson’s responsible business 
commitments and supports resilient opera-
tions and supply chains. It also aligns with 
Ericsson’s ambition to maintain trusted 
­relationships with customers, employees  
and partners, and to contribute to broader 
industry standards on decent work and safe 
employment practices.

Policies
The Code of Business Ethics applies to 
Ericsson’s employees and to any person 
whose work Ericsson exercises day-to-day 
control over. This policy prohibits all forms  
of discrimination, regardless of local legisla-
tion. It recognizes the right to just, safe and 
favorable working conditions, freedom of 
association and collective bargaining, and  
the Company’s commitment to maintaining  
a safe and healthy work environment. It sets 
out Ericsson’s commitment to fair and reason­
able pay, which includes paying, at minimum, 
a living wage to its employees. It strictly pro-
hibits slavery, exploitation, human trafficking, 
child labor and any form of forced or compul-
sory labor. 
Further information about the Code of 
Business Ethics is provided in the section  
 General Disclosures, which also describes 
the main elements of Ericsson’s Business and 
Human Rights Statement. 
Ericsson’s People Policy covers all of its 
employees and individuals performing work 
for Ericsson and sets out the Company’s 
commitment to fair and equitable treatment, 
equal opportunities and good working con-
ditions without discrimination. The policy 
is founded on the principles that every indi-
vidual’s employment opportunity shall be 
based on openness and fairness, that pay and 
recognition shall reward impact and be deter-
mined by market competitiveness, fairness 
and transparency. The policy supports con-
tinuous learning and career development to 
enable employees to upskill and reskill in line 
with evolving business needs. Leaders are 
responsible for fostering an engaging work 
environment where employees can perform 
at their best, grow, feel valued and contribute 
to Ericsson’s long-term success.
The Health, Safety and Wellbeing Policy 
covers employees and, where applicable, 
others affected by the Company’s activities, 
including non-employees within Ericsson’s 
workforce and employees of suppliers. It 
states that Ericsson shall apply a risk-based 
approach to prevent, control and mitigate 
work-related hazards and continually 
improve its management of these matters. 
Ericsson strives to comply with customer and 
other applicable health and safety require-
ments, even when these are stricter than local 
law. Workplaces and processes are designed 
to support health, safety and well-being, 
supported by appropriate tools and training. 
Engagement and consultation with employ-
ees and other stakeholders are carried out 
regularly to support continuous improvement 
of the Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) 
Management System. 
Engagement processes
Engagement with the workforce about actual 
and potential impacts on them takes place 
through several channels. Company-wide 
employee surveys are conducted annually to 
assess work experience, work environment 
and perceptions of leadership and strategy. 
Results are available at Company and unit 
level and can be broken down by employee 
groups to support targeted actions.
Ericsson has established OHS committees 
that include managers and employees, or 
employee representatives where applicable. 
The committees meet regularly, follow up  
on performance and discuss and decide on 
actions to improve the OHS Management 
System and its processes. Information about 
health, safety and well-being targets, perfor-
mance and training is available for all 
employees through internal channels such  
as the intranet and newsletters. In addition, 
all employees are surveyed annually about 
health, safety and well-being, including 
­work-life balance. 
Employees are covered by collective 
­bargaining agreements with workers’ unions 
in several countries where Ericsson operates, 
including countries with a large employee 
headcount such as Sweden, Spain, Romania, 
Hungary, Italy and Brazil. In these countries, 
unions are consulted on matters related to 
working conditions, according to local law.
Ericsson has no global framework agree-
ments with any global union federations but 
maintains dialogue with the Trade Union 
Network, a global union body. Ericsson has 
also established a European Works Council 
that facilitates information and consultation 
between management and employee repre-
sentatives on significant transnational mat-
ters affecting employees in countries within 
the European Economic Area (EEA). 
Ericsson pursues its human rights objec-
tives through collaborations and partnerships 
with other organizations. These initiatives 
support the Company’s human rights due 
diligence and offer additional insight into the 
perspectives of affected stakeholders, includ-
ing its own workforce. The main external col-
laborations, partnerships and commitments 
related to human and labor rights are outlined 
below.
Processes to remediate negative 
impacts and channels to raise concerns
Employees can report suspected violations  
of the Code of Business Ethics, including sus-
pected cases of discrimination, harassment 
and other negative impacts on human and 
labor rights, to their manager, a manager’s 
superior, the People function or the Legal and 
Compliance functions. Concerns can also be 
reported through Ericsson’s Compliance Line, 
which is accessible online or by phone at any 
time and in multiple languages. Anonymous 
reporting is available, and reporters are not 
required to waive their rights to judicial 
­remedies or sign non-disclosure agreements. 
To protect the integrity of the investigations, 
reporters are asked not to share information 
related to ongoing cases. 
Ericsson has in recent years received a 
consistent number of reports through its 
Compliance Line. Many of these concern 
general inquiries rather than potential mis-
conduct or breaches of the Code of Business 
Ethics, laws or regulations, with only a limited 
share of reported concerns leading to inves-
tigations or substantiated findings. This pat-
tern indicates that the reporting channels are 
accessible, well known and trusted. ­Further 
information is provided in the section  
 Business Conduct. 
A central reporting channel is available for 
employees and supplier employees to report 
health and safety incidents and near misses. 
These are handled within a dedicated process 
within the Company’s OHS Management 
System.
When negative impacts are identified, 
Ericsson seeks to provide remedy, for exam-
ple by engaging with affected parties or 
by adapting processes to prevent similar 
occurrences.

Ericsson is committed to providing a safe

address damage and prevent recurrence.

based on a person’s role and risk exposure,

culture.
