the ERM framework and are overseen by the 
Business Risk Committee as needed. A central 
team of human rights experts sets group-level 
priorities, coordinates due diligence and works 
with business areas and regional sales teams 
on human rights initiatives. Human rights 
training is made available to all employees, 
and targeted training and capacity building 
for key job roles and functions are offered. 
Salient human rights issues relate mainly 
to supply-chain workers and potential misuse 
of Ericsson’s technology in the downstream 
value chain. These are addressed in the  
sections 
 Workers in the value chain  
and 
 Consumers and end users. 
For its own operations and workforce, 
Ericsson applies a range of human rights due 
diligence measures in relation to activities or 
operations where risks are assessed to be ele-
vated, in line with the UN Guiding Principles 
on Business and Human Rights and the OECD 
Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. One 
such measure is the use of country visits and 
studies aimed at gaining a deeper understand-
ing of local contexts and potential human 
rights impacts. In recent years, human rights 
experts have conducted visits to operations in 
Mexico and India, engaging in dialogues with 
local employees and management, visiting 
suppliers and organizing meetings and round­
tables with civil society organizations focusing 
on human rights issues of concern to Ericsson. 
The main outcomes of these visits have been 
an increased understanding of country-specific 
operations and related risks, increased aware­
ness of human rights due diligence and identi­
fication of potential negative impacts and 
actions to address them. 
Human rights considerations are also 
included in Ericsson’s due diligence process 
related to mergers, acquisitions and divesti-
tures. The process evaluates the main human

Workforce well-being
Well-being is one component of providing 
adequate working conditions and Ericsson’s 
approach includes a supportive workplace 
environment, job designs that consider physi-
cal, emotional, financial and social well- 
being, and leaders who act as role models for 
safe and healthy behaviors. Hybrid and flexi-
ble working arrangements provide autonomy 
over where and when employees work, fol-
lowing a general office-first guideline while 
allowing flexibility when tasks and responsi-
bilities permit.
Security of workers in high-risk areas 
Ericsson maintains a global framework for 
security in high‑risk areas to support the 
safety of employees, suppliers and con-
tractors operating in locations that could 
be affected by armed conflict, criminality, 
kidnapping, terrorism or civil unrest. The 
Company monitors geopolitical and secu-
rity developments and maintains detailed 
risk assessments. It applies defined travel 
protocols, training, communication systems 
and additional security measures tailored to 
assessed risks. Response plans are in place 
and activated in the event of an emergency  
to ensure coordinated, effective response  
and recovery.
Independent audits of Ericsson’s operations
As a key supplier to many communications 
service providers, Ericsson is periodically 
­subject to third-party audits, including those 
requested by members of the Joint Alliance 
for Corporate Social Responsibility (JAC).  
JAC is a non-profit association of telecom 
operators dedicated to advancing fair working 
conditions and responsible social and environ­
mental practices across the ICT supply chain. 
JAC members conduct joint audits and assess­
ments to verify conformance with sustainabil-
ity standards and to support improvements 
through information-sharing among members.
The audits cover areas such as labor and 
human rights, occupational health and safety, 
environmental management, ethics and man­
agement systems. In recent years, Ericsson’s 
manufacturing facilities in Mexico, China, 
Romania, Estonia and the United States have 
been audited. Overall, the results indicate that 
Ericsson meets the audit criteria. However, 
findings were identified in certain areas, pri-
marily related to working hours. These have 
been addressed through engagement with 
affected employees and local corrective 
action plans, and the actions are monitored 
on an ongoing basis.

Health and safety 
Ericsson had a target of zero work-related fatalities and lost workday 
incidents caused by work-related physical injuries or work-related 
illnesses within the Company’s control by 2025. This target covered 
both own workforce and employees of field service suppliers.
OHS experts, in collaboration with key internal stakeholders, monitor 
progress toward this and related sub-targets to identify actions for 
improvement. These targets are included in regular internal manage-
ment reporting to the Executive Team.
In 2025, there were 3 fatalities and 60 lost workday incidents com-
pared with 2 and 72 respectively in 2024. All fatalities occurred among 
supplier personnel, and 38 of the lost workday incidents occurred 
within Ericsson’s own workforce. Ericsson recognizes the seriousness 
of this outcome. Achieving a zero-incident target is challenging, as 
incidents arise from a combination of human factors and complex 
operational environments. The Company will continue to prioritize 
the highest-consequence risks, strengthen safety programs, including 
contractor and supplier management, and ensure consistent leader­
ship attention, resourcing and accountability. These efforts aim to 
further reduce the likelihood of fatalities and lost workday incidents. 
Reducing and ultimately eliminating work-related accidents remains  
a central focus of Ericsson’s health and safety efforts.
With the exception of the health and safety target, Ericsson has  
not set targets for material impacts related to its own workforce. The 
Company continues to assess the appropriateness of target setting as 
part of its management approach. The effectiveness of related policies 
and actions is, in part, monitored through workforce-related KPIs, 
including those disclosed in the Sustainability Statement.

Other work-related rights 
Forced labor remains a potential negative 
impact in several stages of the global elec-
tronics supply chain, including raw material 
extraction, smelting and component manu-
facturing, particularly in Central and Eastern 
Africa, South and Southeast Asia, East Asia 
and Latin America. Contributing factors 
include weak enforcement of labor laws, 
exploitation of migrant workers, debt bondage 
and excessive overtime. 
Ericsson’s exposure to child labor is 
considered lower and is primarily linked to 
specific high-risk minerals, such as cobalt 
and mica extracted in countries including 
the Democratic Republic of the Congo and 
Madagascar2). Although Ericsson does not 
source raw materials directly, these minerals 
are used in the components and products it 
procures. This means that Ericsson’s business 
model, which depends on global electronics 
manufacturing, is inherently linked to such 
potential and negative impacts, which may 
occur several tiers upstream in its value chain. 
Workers most exposed include those in 
mineral extraction and processing, as well as 
sub-supplier factory workers in electronics 
manufacturing hubs. Ericsson identifies these 
risks through supplier assessments, industry 
initiatives and external risk-mapping tools, 
which guide its due diligence priorities. Expo-
sure to these systemic human rights-related 
impacts is current and is expected to persist 
over the medium to long term. 
While not considered financially material, 
evolving regulations, including the EU Corpo-
rate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, 
the EU Forced Labour Regulation and US 
anti-forced labor import bans, together with 
rising customer expectations, require compa-
nies to strengthen due diligence practices. 
Non-compliance could result in restricted 
market access, legal or reputational conse-
quences or reduced competitiveness in 
­customer purchasing decisions.

The Code of Conduct for Business Partners 
requires business partners, such as suppliers, 
to respect all internationally recognized human 
rights standards, including the International 
Bill of Human Rights and International Labor 
Organization (ILO). Business partners must: 
provide clear, written employment agreements, 
ensure employees do not pay recruitment 
fees and allow migrant workers access to 
identification or immigration documents. 
Forced, bonded and child labor are prohibited. 
Young employees under the age of 18 must 
not perform work that is likely to jeopardize 
their health or safety, including night shifts 
and overtime. Working hours must comply 
with local laws, not exceed 60 hours per week 
including overtime, and should strive toward 
the ILO standard of 48 hours per week. 
Employees must earn a living wage that 
meets basic needs and allows for some dis-
cretionary income. Workplaces must be free 
from unlawful discrimination, harassment or 
inhumane treatment, and employees should 
have the right to form unions and engage in 
collective bargaining.
Ericsson offers free training on the Code of 
Conduct to its suppliers. In addition, targeted 
content covering anti-corruption, human 
rights, conflict minerals and OHS is available 
on the Company’s website, which also pro-
vides access to the United Nations Global 
Compact Academy for employees in 
Ericsson’s sourcing organization.
The Code requires business partners to 
implement a risk-based approach to health 
and safety, provide relevant training, and 
maintain incident reporting and corrective 
action processes. They are also required to 
have an OHS management system. Specific 
OHS standards apply to suppliers involved in 
construction, field maintenance and network 
rollout, including requirements for managing 
subcontractors.
Further information on the Code of Con-
duct for Business Partners is provided in the 
section 
 General disclosures, which also 
describes the main elements of Ericsson’s 
Business and Human Rights Statement.
Engagement processes
Ericsson uses direct and indirect channels 
to engage with workers in its value chain on 
actual and potential impacts affecting them. 
The Code of Conduct Audit Program, which 
targets suppliers, includes worker interviews 
focused on human and labor rights and is 
described below. 
Ericsson regularly engages with organiza-
tions as proxies for the views of workers in the 
value chain. This includes membership in the 
Shift Business Learning Program to promote 
business respect for human rights according 
to the United Nations Guiding Principles for 
Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), the 
Business Network on Civic Freedoms and 
Human Rights Defenders, and the Responsible 
Business Alliance (RBA). 
Heightened due diligence activities involve 
direct engagement with labor rights organiza­
tions and roundtables with civil society and 
other stakeholders as relevant. Ericsson is 
working closely with the Responsible Minerals 
Initiative (RMI) and participates in its working 
groups, where it chairs the Aluminum Working 
Group.
Processes to remediate negative 
impacts and channels to raise concerns
Findings from supplier audits are addressed 
through time-bound corrective action plans, 
making them a key mechanism for reme-
diating negative impacts on value-chain 
workers. Workers can report concerns about 
violations of the Code of Conduct for Business 
Partners, policies, laws or regulation through 
the Ericsson Compliance Line, which is avail-
able to internal and external stakeholders, 
including suppliers and their employees (see 
the section 
 Business conduct). Business 
partners must maintain their own grievance 
mechanisms that enable employees to raise 
concerns safely and without fear of reprisal or 
retaliation.
	 In 2025, no severe negative human rights 
impacts related to workers in the value chain 
were reported through Ericsson’s channels, 
and no remediation actions were therefore 
undertaken.
Management actions
Ericsson is committed to conducting business 
responsibly and has established several pro-
cesses to manage impacts on workers in its 
value chain. The key actions described below 
relate to: supplier screening and auditing, crit-
ical minerals and supply-chain traceability, 
and supplier health and safety management. 
Supplier screening and auditing
A dedicated unit within Ericsson’s sourcing 
organization drives sustainability and cor-
porate responsibility initiatives, focusing on 
­supplier compliance with the Code of Conduct 
for Business Partners via risk assessments 
and dedicated Code of Conduct audits. 
Suppliers must agree to the Code of 
Conduct before entering into business with 
Ericsson, and first-tier suppliers are assessed 
for risks of nonconformity regarding its pro-
visions. New suppliers are screened and 
selected based on multiple criteria, includ-
ing environmental and social factors, using 
third-party databases to identify instances 
of adverse media, instances of regulatory 
non-compliance, anticompetitive behavior, 
financial irregularities, as well as environ-
ment, production, and labor and human-
rights issues.
A modular supplier-sustainability risk 
assessment may be activated depending  
on the supplier’s risk profile, with the scope 
determined by the type of products or services 
provided. When a supplier is selected for 
assessment, relevant self-assessment ques-
tionnaires covering environmental, health 
and safety and human-rights management 
topics are sent for completion.
Following the assessment, suppliers 
receive a risk rating, and based on the outcome, 
a recommendation is made to approve, not 
approve, or approve the supplier with specific 
conditions to address identified gaps (or the 
equivalent recommendations for active sup-
pliers). Once onboarded, suppliers are contin-
uously screened for adverse media coverage 
at regular intervals. 
When initial screenings or assessments 
identify potentially elevated human-rights 
risks, Ericsson conducts heightened human-
rights due diligence to further evaluate and 
address these risks. The process may include 
desktop studies of the security and regulatory 
environment, forced-labor screenings using 
third-party risk data providers, and engage-
ment with peers through channels such as the 
Responsible Business Alliance or Responsible 
Minerals Initiative. Ericsson may also consult 
civil-society organizations or other external 
stakeholders to better understand local con-
texts. Where heightened risks are confirmed, 
Ericsson works with first-tier suppliers to 
reinforce Code of Conduct requirements and 
may require external audits and time-bound 
corrective action plans. The human rights- 
focused country visits described in the section 
 Own workforce also covered matters 
related to workers in the value chain.
Ericsson audits its first-tier suppliers to 
verify compliance with the Code of Conduct. 
These audits focus on suppliers identified as 
having heightened environmental, human-
rights, labor or business-conduct-related 
risks. In scope for selection are primarily 
suppliers that fall within the top 90% total 
procurement spend. Supplier risk, determined 
by factors such as country, product or service 
type, time since last audit and purchase 
volume, guides the audit selection process. 
Audits are conducted by an external provider, 
mainly on-site, with remote audits used for 
high-risk countries or follow-ups. Focus areas 
include employment conditions, working 
hours, wages, health and safety, chemical 
handling and the supplier’s communication of 
requirements to their own suppliers.
Nonconformities must be resolved through 
time-bound corrective action plans. Audits 
are not conducted on an unannounced basis, 
but semi-announced audits are carried out, 
where suppliers are informed that an audit 
will occur within a defined time frame without 
disclosure of the exact date and time.

Critical minerals and supply-chain 
­traceability 
Ericsson has no direct purchasing relation­
ships with companies involved in the extrac­tion, 
smelting or refining of minerals. Its exposure 
to raw materials, including conflict minerals, 
is indirect, through the materials and miner-
als used in components forming part of the 
electronic hardware sold in network solutions. 
This indirect exposure makes thorough due 
diligence and industry collaboration essential 
to managing related risks.
Ericsson is committed to sourcing critical 
minerals, including tantalum, tungsten, lithium 
and nickel, in compliance with all applicable 
legislation. The Company’s due diligence 
measures align with the OECD Due Diligence 
Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of 
Minerals and comply with emerging regula-
tions such as the EU Battery Regulation and 
the Critical Raw Materials Act.
Suppliers of electronic hardware are required 
to conduct due diligence on the sourcing and 
extraction of critical minerals and to verify, with 
reasonable certainty, the origin of minerals in 
products supplied to Ericsson. Traceability 
beyond first-tier suppliers is pursued primarily 
via engagement in industry networks and 
associations, using tools and templates of the 
RMI to map supply chains and identify smelters 
and refiners. Ericsson also uses RMI assessment 
data on identified smelters and refiners to deter­
mine whether enhanced due diligence or supplier 
collaboration is warranted.
Ericsson seeks to increase sourcing from 
suppliers and sub-suppliers that meet rele-
vant minerals-sustainability standards, such 
as those of the RMI. The Company uses the 
RMI framework, working groups and tools to 
engage directly with smelters where no direct 
business relationship exists, or to strengthen 
requirements on sub-suppliers through direct 
suppliers. Ericsson strives to work collabora­
tively with suppliers toward continuous 
improvement but may terminate business 
relationships as a last resort in case of recur-
ring noncompliance.
Further details are provided in Ericsson’s 
annual Conflict Minerals Report on Form SD, 
published on its website and filed with the 
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
Supplier health and safety management 
Ericsson has established global requirements 
for field service suppliers as part of its Code of 
Conduct for Business Partners. Key require-
ments are incident reporting and investiga-
tion, hazard and risk management, commu-
nication and awareness, Stop Work Authority 
and mandatory training. The Stop Work 
Authority requires and empowers personnel 
to immediately stop work when unsafe condi-
tions are identified. 
Through supplier safety maturity assess-
ments, Ericsson evaluates site service sup-
pliers against predefined health and safety 
criteria. Based on the results, improvement 
plans must be completed within set time-
frames, and new suppliers must successfully 
complete the assessment before onboarding. 
For active suppliers, follow-up assessments 
aim to drive improvement in safety perfor-
mance. Suppliers must complete mandatory 
training courses defined by Ericsson, includ-
ing health and safety induction, safe driving 
awareness and lifesaving rules. 
Consequence management applies when 
suppliers fail to close actions within agreed 
time frames, decline to participate in assess-
ments or breach Ericsson’s safety require-
ments. Possible measures include financial 
penalties, reduced business volumes, addi-
tional inspections or audits, written warnings 
or, in severe cases, termination of the supplier 
relationship. Health and safety measures 
described in the section 
 Own workforce 
also apply to site service supplier employees.
In 2025, Ericsson continued to conduct 
Target Zero workshops to strengthen safety 
culture across its supply base, and implemen­
ted a Supplier Safety Recognition Program to 
further promote safe behavior. Under this pro-
gram, suppliers were recognized locally and 
globally in three categories: safe behavior, best 
practice and top improvement suggestion. 
Maturity assessments for site-service suppli-
ers continued in 2025, focusing on improving 
safety maturity and evaluating new suppliers.
Targets
Ericsson has a target for zero fatalities and 
lost-workday incidents, which covers both its 
own workforce and employees of site service 
suppliers. Further information about this target 
is provided in the section

With the exception of the health and 
safety target, Ericsson has not set additional 
targets for material impacts related to work-

the appropriateness of target setting as part 
of its management approach. For direct sup-
pliers, the effectiveness of related policies  
and actions is, in part, monitored through  
the supplier audits described above.

Misuse of technology
Ericsson’s technologies are designed to  
provide secure and reliable connectivity,  
but they may also be used in ways that could 
negatively affect consumers and end users 
depending on the context and actors involved. 
Potential negative impacts include breaches 
of privacy rights, for example through surveil-
lance of private communications, and restric-
tions on freedom of expression, such as the 
blocking or filtering of online content.
These impacts can arise when network 
features, such as performance management 
functions, are used beyond their intended 
legitimate purpose, including by authorities. 
In some contexts, Ericsson may also be indi-
rectly required to support temporary network 
shutdowns when operating networks on behalf 
of customers. Ericsson does not receive such 
requests directly, but misuse downstream can 
still affect the rights of people who depend on 
the networks.
These impacts are not limited to specific 
groups of end users. Their likelihood and 
severity depend on the broader context, 
including the strength of human rights pro-
tections, legal and regulatory frameworks, 
rule of law and democratic institutions in 
the countries where the technologies are 
deployed. They are current and expected  
to persist over the medium to long term.
Like network security, preventing the 
­misuse of technology supports trust in digital 
infrastructure. Ericsson’s approach includes 
human rights due diligence, contractual 
safeguards, technical mitigations and stake-
holder engagement to help identify risks of 
misuse and support responsible use of its 
technologies.
Network security
Ericsson’s networks carry an estimated 50% 
of global mobile 5G traffic outside China, 
making their security and reliability critical for 
consumers and end users worldwide. These 
networks handle sensitive personal data and 
support essential services such as health care, 
utilities and public safety. Therefore, a data 
breach or disruption can result in negative 
effects on individuals and society. These are 
potential negative impacts that are current 
and likely to persist over the medium to long 
term.
These impacts are linked to Ericsson’s role 
in delivering critical connectivity infrastructure. 
Ensuring robust security safeguards is there-
fore central to maintaining customer confi-
dence and supporting secure and reliable 
­networks. No specific vulnerable groups have 
been identified, as these issues affect all 
types of end users due to the widespread 
­reliance on connectivity.
Failures in network security, such as 
unplanned outages or the exposure of sensi­
tive data, can result in reputational harm, 
contractual issues or deployment delays. In 
severe cases, they may lead to loss of business, 
making network security a financially material 
risk as well as a consumer and end-user impact. 
This risk is current and expected to persist 
over the medium to long term. Addressing 
these concerns is an integral part of Ericsson’s 
strategy and is embedded in its approach to 
supporting resilience in critical infrastructure.
Policies
The Code of Business Ethics outlines 
Ericsson’s commitment to respect freedom 
of expression and privacy and requires the 
mitigation of risks related to the misuse of 
technology. Employees must assess external 
requests that may affect these rights and 
verify that such requests are legitimate, pro-
portionate and necessary before responding. 
Internal procedures to mitigate associated 
risks must be followed, and concerns must be 
raised if risks are overlooked or insufficiently 
addressed. Ericsson is a member of the Global 
Network Initiative (GNI) and adheres to its 
Principles on Freedom of Expression and 
­Privacy. Further information about the Code 
of Business Ethics is provided in the section  
 General disclosures, which also describes 
the main elements of Ericsson’s Business and 
Human Rights Statement. 
The Development, Innovation and Use  
of Technology Policy sets out Ericsson’s com-
mitment to the responsible, compliant and 
ethical use of technology. It provides guid-
ance across the design, development, sale, 
deployment and use of Ericsson’s products 
and aims to ensure that technology-related 
decisions are appropriately considered and 
that potential risks, including ethical and 
human rights risks, are identified, assessed 
and addressed.
Ericsson maintains a Company-wide 
security policy that aims to prevent, detect, 
respond to, remediate data and recover from 
breaches and infrastructure disruption that 
affect its networks and services. Further infor-
mation is provided in the subsection Security 
policy on page 20 of the Board of Directors’ 
report.

Corporate culture, anti-bribery  
and ­corruption 
Ericsson serves customers in more than 175 
countries, including markets with elevated 
exposure to bribery and corruption due to 
weaker societal institutions. The telecommuni­
cations sector has elevated risk because of its 
technical complexity and close interaction 
with both public and private stakeholders.
Ericsson has previously admitted to viola­
tions of anti-bribery and corruption laws, 
which resulted in significant fines, increased 
compliance costs and reputational impact. 
Over four years, the Company operated under 
an independent compliance monitorship, 
which officially concluded in 2024, following 
certification that its Ethics & Compliance 
­Program meets required standards. Ericsson 
continues to emphasize the importance of a 
sound corporate culture and has strengthened 
its program accordingly. Nevertheless, recur­
rence of unlawful or unethical behavior 
remains a financially material risk. Potential 
consequences include legal penalties, 
increased operating costs, and harm to 
­customer trust and market position.
This risk is directly connected to Ericsson’s 
global operating model and is expected to 
persist over the medium to long term. Monitor­
ing, prevention and continuous enhancement 
of the Ethics & Compliance Program and 
­corporate culture remain integral parts of 
Ericsson’s governance and risk management.
Political engagement and lobbying 
­activities
Ericsson operates in a wide range of regula­
tory and geopolitical environments. The tele­
communications sector is highly regulated 
and increasingly politicized, shifts in policy, 
regulation or geopolitical alignments can 
affect Ericsson’s market access, supply chains 
and R&D activities. Examples of policy areas 
of relevance include spectrum, competition, 
trade and cybersecurity. While engaging with 
public authorities and industry associations is 
a normal part of business, engagement that 
is unsuccessful or inadequately managed can 
result in unfavorable policies or reputational 
harm. Such unwanted outcomes may pose 
financially material risks for Ericsson and are 
expected to persist over the medium to long 
term. The Company addresses these risks 
through governance controls, oversight of 
advocacy efforts and transparency regarding 
its policy engagements.
Management of relationships with ­suppliers 
including payment practices
As a major purchaser of components, products 
and services in the global ICT sector, Ericsson 
recognizes that its scale and market position 
may influence the balance of power in supplier 
relationships. If not managed proactively, this 
could lead to contractual terms and conditions 
that are challenging for some suppliers and 
may affect their financial stability, capacity  
to invest or long-term operational resilience.
These potential negative impacts are con­
centrated upstream in the value chain and 
may be more relevant to smaller or highly 
specialized suppliers. They are current and 
expected to persist over the medium to long 
term. Such pressures may weaken supplier 
resilience and, in turn, may affect the continuity, 
quality and sustainability of Ericsson’s supply 
chain. Ericsson therefore monitors supplier 
relationships and integrates these consider­
ations into its sourcing practices. This includes 
promoting fair and transparent contracting, 
engaging in dialogue to understand supplier 
constraints and applying differentiated 
approaches where appropriate.
Maintaining balanced and constructive 
supplier relationships is essential not only for 
responsible business conduct and long-term 
supply-chain stability. Resilient relationships 
also support continuity of supply, which is 
increasingly important given ongoing geo­
political uncertainties.
Policies and ­corporate culture
The Code of Business Ethics sets out the 
Company’s values and provides a framework 
for ethical decision-making and risk manage­
ment. It covers various areas such as bribery, 
corruption, financial fraud, conflicts of interest, 
harassment and anticompetitive practices. 
Ericsson also provides additional and more 
detailed guidance on topics such as: anti-­
corruption, gifts, entertainment and hospitality, 
third-party management, conflicts of interest, 
anti-money laundering, antitrust law and 
insider trading rules. 
The Code of Conduct for Business Partners 
requires suppliers to uphold a culture of integ­
rity based on transparency, compliance and 
ethical business practices. Further information 
regarding the Code of Business Ethics and 
Code of Conduct for Business Partners is 
included in the section 
 General disclosures.
Ericsson’s Group Policy on Government 
and Policy Advocacy requires anticipating, 
analyzing, managing and mitigating political, 
regulatory and reputational risks. The policy 
commits the Company to conduct government 
and policy advocacy with transparency, integ­
rity and ethics. 
Channels for reporting  
compliance ­concerns
Employees are expected to report compliance 
concerns, so that these can be assessed and 
addressed to identify, prevent and remediate 
misconduct and gaps in internal controls. 
Ericsson’s Compliance Line is a dedicated 
communication channel for employees and 
external stakeholders to report any compliance 
concerns via a secure website or by phone.  
It is operated by a third party, accessible at 
any time and supports reporting from multiple 
countries in several languages, including 
anonymously where permitted by law. During 
the year, reports have been received from third 
parties, indicating that external stakeholders 
are aware and make use of this channel.
Where applicable, employees and external 
stakeholders can also report concerns via local 
channels established under the EU Whistle­
blower Directive. Employees may additionally 
raise concerns directly with their manager, the 
manager’s superior or to the People or Legal 
and Compliance departments. Retaliation 
against individuals who report compliance 
concerns in good faith is not tolerated.

Prevention and detection  
of corruption and bribery
Risk assessments 
Ericsson’s Ethics and Compliance Program 
maintains a risk-based approach. In 2025, 
14 compliance and integrity risk assessments 
were concluded across selected regional sales 
units and business units, focusing on regions 
and operations with elevated exposure based 
on risk and business context. 
These assessments help identify and 
address key compliance and integrity risks 
across areas such as sales practices, third-
party management, gifts and hospitality, 
­government interactions, sponsorships and 
donations, conflicts of interest and human 
rights. They include elements such as leader­
ship and culture, and how risks are understood, 
owned and managed within the business. In 
2025, the scope was expanded to also assess 
broader risk themes, including fraud, sanctions 
and export controls, reflecting a shifting 
external landscape. 
To ensure accountability and timely reme­
diation, the status of remediation actions 
identified in risk assessments is tracked in  
a dedicated tool that provides end-to-end 
­visibility from initial findings to closure. 
Third-party management 
Ericsson maintains a global, risk-based third-
party management program to prevent, detect 
and manage risks, including anti-bribery risks, 
in its relationships with third parties. Compli­
ance risk management is integrated into 
­business processes, with business leaders, 
managers and employees all expected to act 
as owners of compliance risk. A central team 
of due diligence and data specialists manages 
key elements such as risk-based assessments 
to evaluate risk exposure and potential liabil­
ity that may result from relationships with 
third parties. 
A range of risk mitigation measures can  
be applied where elevated risks are identified, 
including targeted training, third-party certifi­
cations, financial transaction pre-approvals 
and, in severe cases, payment blocks or rejec­
tions. Ericsson also periodically exercises its 
audit rights and performs external checks 
within its supply chain to verify that third 
­parties conduct business appropriately.
During 2025, additional risk indicators 
were added to the third-party management 
procedures to further improve country-level 
assessments, including factoring in risks of 
organized crime and money laundering.
Addressing compliance concerns
Ericsson provides multiple channels for 
employees and external stakeholders to 
report suspected violations of policies or laws. 
Reported compliance concerns are received 
and initially assessed by a dedicated, cen­
tralized team, and cases that require further 
investigation are referred to a specialized 
investigations team. 
The teams responsible for assessing, 
investigating and driving remediation of 
­compliance concerns belong to Ericsson’s 
Compliance Office and Investigations unit, 
which is independent of the business and 
regional sales functions. This unit is led by the 
Head of Compliance Office and Investigations, 
who reports to the Chief Legal Officer and who 
has an independent reporting line to the Audit 
and Compliance Committee of the Board of 
Directors. Reporting to the Committee 
includes information on actual or suspected 
serious violations of the Code of Business 
Ethics, insights from investigation outcomes 
and remediation measures, identified patterns 
and trends, and emerging risks or develop­
ments in the legal and regulatory 
environment.
Communication of anti-bribery  
and corruption policies
Employees receive Ericsson’s Code of Business 
Ethics during onboarding and must confirm 
their understanding and commitment at that 
time and on an annual basis thereafter, unless 
otherwise decided by the Executive Team. 
This regular reaffirmation supports ongoing 
awareness of and adherence to the Company’s 
ethical standards.
To support continuous learning and ethical 
awareness, Ericsson publishes the Integrity 
Insider, a global internal newsletter that pres­
ents anonymous cases of misconduct, exam­
ples of ethical lessons from other companies or 
enforcement actions and highlights colleagues 
who have demonstrated behaving with integ­
rity. It also includes conversation starters that 
can be used by employees and teams to have 
meaningful conversations about integrity. The 
newsletter is one of the Company’s most-read 
internal publications and reinforces awareness 
of expected conduct and consequences for 
misconduct.

Political influence and  
lobbying ­activities
Ericsson participates in national and trans­
national trade associations and industry 
organizations that are aligned with its values 
and maintains consistent policy positions. 
The Company does not contribute to political 
parties or individual politicians, except for 
supporting voluntary employee contributions 
permitted by local law and reporting

Ericsson is a member of several associations 
and chambers of commerce on a national

mine its commitment to ethical business 
practices. All new or renewed memberships

ciples apply when employees participate in

objectives.

ment, and the head of that unit occasionally

Management of relationships

Payment practices
Ericsson, with more than 15,000 active direct 
suppliers, seeks to apply transparent, fair and 
responsible payment practices. The Company 
works to maintain processes that support 
timely and accurate payments in line with 
contractual commitments and applicable 
legal requirements.
On average, invoices are paid within 81 
days from the start of the contractual or 
statutory payment term. Standard contrac­
tual payment terms, as set out in Ericsson’s 
purchasing conditions, are 120 days. Actual 
terms can vary by country, regulatory require­
ments, financing arrangements and commer­
cial agreements.
Ericsson segments its supplier base by 
agreed payment term ranges: less than 60 
days, 60 to 120 days and more than 120 
days. Invoices from 74 of the top 100 suppliers 
by spend, representing 84% of procurement 
value, are settled within 120 days, which 
aligns with the Company’s global standard 
contractual terms. 
Payment terms are established through 
dialogue with suppliers to ensure a fair and 
responsible approach that considers the 
needs of large enterprises as well as small 
and medium-sized suppliers. Internal records 
indicate that no formal legal cases related to 
late payments were identified in the reporting 
period. Average contractual terms and pay­
ment times are calculated using a weighted 
methodology based on invoice values.
Taxes and transfer pricing
Serving customers in more than 175 countries, 
Ericsson acknowledges the societal impor­
tance of taxes in supporting sustainable 
development.
Ericsson sees taxes as a responsibility 
that contributes to socioeconomic develop­
ment, along with employment creation, use 
of local suppliers and other direct and indi­
rect economic impacts. However, Ericsson’s 
global presence exposes it to complex tax 
regulations that may be subject to varying 
interpretation. 
The Company’s policy is to comply with 
both the intent and the requirements of all 
applicable tax laws, managing taxes with 
integrity, accuracy and transparency, while 
maintaining open relationships with tax 
authorities.
Ericsson adheres to both local tax laws 
and international guidelines set forth by the 
OECD and other standard-setting and regula­
tory bodies, including the arm’s-length princi­
ple. Ericsson does not engage in tax practices 
lacking economic substance and does not 
use low-tax jurisdictions for tax-planning 
purposes. 
AI governance 
Ericsson aims to accelerate the adoption of AI 
in an ethical, responsible and compliant man­
ner to safeguard the interests and security of 
the Company and its stakeholders, including 
its workforce and customers. AI is used across 
the Company, in various activities including 
product development and deployment, and 
internal processes. 
A dedicated cross-functional program for 
responsible AI has been established to pro­
vide a framework for risk management and 
governance, anchored in Ericsson’s Develop­
ment, Innovation and Use of Technology 
Policy, which sets out the Company’s founda­
tional approach to AI. As an example, fairness 
is one of the core principles, encouraging 
ethical and inclusive AI use and mitigation 
of potentially discriminatory or biased out­
comes. All employees engaged with AI must 
adhere to these foundational principles and 
requirements. 
Ericsson aligns with applicable regulation 
and other frameworks such as the EU’s AI Act, 
the OECD’s AI Principles and the EU’s Ethics 
Guidelines for Trustworthy AI. The Company 
also offers foundational AI training to its 
workforce to promote adoption, responsible 
use and risk awareness.

Risk factors
This Risk factors section should be read in conjunction with all of 
the information contained in this Annual Report, including this 
Financial Report and the consolidated financial statements and 
accompanying notes.
Ericsson’s business is subject to a number of risks and 
uncertainties that may affect its business, operating results 
and financial condition, or the trading price of its common stock 
or other securities. Ericsson cautions the reader that these risk 
factors may not be exhaustive. Ericsson operates in a continually 
changing business and regulatory environment, and new risks 
and uncertainties emerge from time to time. Management cannot 
predict such new risks and uncertainties, nor can it assess the extent 
to which any of the risk factors below or any such new risks and 
uncertainties, or any combination thereof, may impact Ericsson’s 
business. See also ”Forward-Looking Statements”.
1  Risks related to business activities and industry
1.1  Ongoing geopolitical and trade uncertainty from a range of 
­factors may have a material adverse impact on Ericsson’s business, 
operations, and ability to meet its targets, as well as the information 
and telecommunications industry as a whole. 
Geopolitical alliances are shifting as global tensions over trade and 
influence drive growing economic, technological, military, and polit-
ical competition across the world, particularly between the US and 
China. Geopolitical tensions and ongoing conflicts such as those in the 
broader Middle East, Russia and Ukraine, amplify the risk of govern-
ment intervention, including state-based armed conflicts and protec-
tionist interventions, such as tariffs, and security-related requirements, 
which include increased regulatory barriers, restrictions on technology 
transfers, telecommunications and digital infrastructure to promote 
national security, as well as trade restrictions, export controls and 
enhanced sanctions measures. Additionally, geopolitical instability 
increasingly leads some governments to use the private sector for 
political objectives, including by restricting or enabling market access 
based on national security interests, leveraging influence over indus-
try standards, providing financial support to domestic companies 
or restricting the use of foreign equipment or technology in critical 
infrastructure. 
Many countries, including the US and China, view technology, 
including telecommunications infrastructure and mobile wireless tech-
nologies, as critical infrastructure and aim to lead and influence global 
policy and regulations around such technologies. Due to the strategic 
nature of the industry in which Ericsson operates, foreign countries 
could support a competitor as a national champion or develop a 
national champion as an alternative to the established global vendors, 
such as Ericsson, in order to have further control over local commu-
nication networks and infrastructure. Additionally, foreign countries 
could support or establish a national champion competitor in markets 
of strategic importance to Ericsson, such as the US, India and Japan, 
resulting in a loss of market share and global scale. Collaborative 
arrangements between competitors and influential technology part-
ners or national stakeholders could shape public perception, influ-
encing national champion narratives in certain markets. In particular, 
strategic alliances between competitors and influential technology 
partners, or the emergence of a favored national champion competi-
tor, could prompt policy preferences, trade measures or procurement 
decisions from interested governments that favor those competitors 
irrespective of technical merit, heightening geopolitical and trade 
uncertainty and potentially impairing Ericsson’s market share, access 
to critical components or government contracts. 
While Ericsson is a global company with a global presence, it 
faces unique challenges as a Swedish company because Sweden and 
Europe have historically exerted limited influence in shaping global 
technology policies compared to more prominent technology regula-
tors and have not committed similar levels of investment in technology 
infrastructure. Neither Sweden nor the European Union has developed 
a common and cohesive technology agenda or technology geopo-
litical strategy. Where regulations in the European Union have been 
introduced, such regulations have focused on consumer pricing, rather 
than promoting or protecting European-based technology or telecom-
munications companies. Consequently, Ericsson remains exposed to 
changes in global policy dynamics that it cannot directly or indirectly 
influence, and which may be influenced to benefit competitors. Fur-
thermore, as a Swedish company operating globally during a period of 
rapidly evolving government and regulatory priorities, and, in certain 
cases, conflicting or changing requirements (including, for example, 
regarding environmental, climate and diversity and inclusion policies), 
Ericsson may be required to make operational adjustments, which 
impair its ability to implement consistent global policies, expose it to 
enforcement or litigation risk, and harm its reputation or brand.
Due to the strategic nature of the information and telecommunica-
tions industry, Ericsson is exposed to competitive risks from state-sup-
ported enterprises, particularly from countries with significant govern-
ment-backed industries. Companies in government-backed industries 
may receive financial support, favorable regulatory environments, 
the advantage of a closed home market and selective enforcement of 
rules that enable them to operate at a scale and with a cost structure 
that private sector companies cannot match. They may also receive 
market and technology access that grants them significant compet-
itive advantages. This dynamic can create competitive pressures, 
particularly in international markets where these government-sup-
ported enterprises can operate with significantly lower margins com-
pared to private sector companies. Additionally, such state-backed 
entities may pursue opportunities in pursuit of strategic objectives of 
their government owners and supporters, with less focus on financial 
returns, allowing for these companies to increase their market share 
disproportionately.

periods of elevated interest rates or inflation, fluctuations in currency 
exchange rates, falling consumer confidence, or geopolitical risks and 
trade frictions may have adverse, wide-ranging effects on demand 
for Ericsson’s products and for the products and services of Ericsson’s 
customers. These conditions are also impacted by government fiscal 
and monetary policies, including adverse changes relating to gov-
ernment grants, tax credits or other government incentives. Ericsson 
operates in a cyclical industry, where customer demand, investment 
and spending are highly sensitive to macroeconomic conditions, fluc-
tuating market dynamics and broader investment cycles. If Ericsson’s 
customers anticipate or experience reduced consumer spending, 
communications service provider customers and other customers 
may postpone, reduce or cancel investments, including significantly 
reduced expenditures for the Company’s products and services, or ini-
tiate other cost-cutting measures to maintain or improve their finan-
cial position. This reduced demand for products and services could 
result in increased price competition or deferrals of purchases, leading 
to lower revenues not fully offset by reduced costs. If Ericsson’s finan-
cial performance is constrained due to an economic downturn, its 
ability to reinvest in product innovation, market expansion, or other 
strategic initiatives important to Ericsson’s long-term growth could be 
limited. Furthermore, if economic conditions lead to reduced invest-
ment in technology sectors broadly, Ericsson’s growth prospects could 
be adversely impacted.

5.1  Failure to comply with environmental, human rights, business 
conduct and occupational health and safety regulations and laws in 
applicable jurisdictions may expose Ericsson to significant penalties 
and other sanctions or liabilities.
Ericsson is subject to environmental, human rights, business conduct 
and occupational health and safety laws, rules and regulations as 
well as related requirements, which apply to Ericsson’s operations, 
facilities, products and services. Ericsson expects these laws, rules 
and regulations, and the resources needed for complying with them 
to increase as governments impose new laws, rules, regulations and 
other requirements or amend existing ones. Ericsson’s measures for 
managing compliance with these laws, rules, regulations and other 
requirements may not be effective at avoiding potential liabilities aris-
ing from Ericsson’s current, historical and future processes, operations 
and business relationships.
Ericsson has failed to comply with some of these laws, rules, reg-
ulations and other requirements in the past, and if it fails to comply in 
the future, the Company could be subject to significant penalties and 
other sanctions or liabilities that could have a material adverse effect 
on Ericsson. If suppliers do not adhere to Ericsson’s Code of Conduct 
for Business Partners and laws related to environmental, human 
rights, business conduct or occupational health and safety, this could 
also have a material adverse effect on Ericsson. Additionally, there 
is a risk that Ericsson may have to incur expenditures to cover envi-
ronmental, human rights, occupational health and safety liabilities to 
maintain compliance with current or future applicable laws and regu-
lations or to undertake any necessary remediation. Future regulations 
or judgments, as well as any change in interpretation of existing laws, 
could have a significant adverse effect on Ericsson. These changing 
rules, regulations, and requirements have resulted, and are likely to 
result in increased general and administrative expenses and increased 
management time and attention. For example, developing and act-
ing on environmental, social and business conduct initiatives, and 
collecting, measuring, auditing and reporting environmental, social 
and business conduct information and metrics can be costly, difficult 
and time consuming and is subject to evolving disclosure standards. 
Failure to meet applicable diversity, equity and inclusion regulations, 
rules and requirements, workforce reporting obligations or evolving 
stakeholder expectations, including disclosure and non-discrimination 
rules, regulations and requirements, could expose Ericsson to regula-
tory enforcement, litigation, decreased access to talent, reduced cus-
tomer or investor confidence, and reputational harm. Failure to man-
age the foregoing risks could furthermore have an adverse impact on 
Ericsson’s business, operating results, financial condition, reputation 
and brand. 
New environmental, human rights, occupational health and safety 
laws, rules, regulations and standards are being developed, such as 
those related to climate change and the potential environmental 
impact resulting therefrom, that may affect the Company, its suppli-
ers, and its customers. Such laws, rules, regulations and standards 
could cause Ericsson to incur additional direct costs for compliance, 
including costs associated with changes to manufacturing processes, 
or costs associated with the procurement of raw materials and com-
ponents used in Ericsson’s products, as well as increased indirect costs 
resulting from its suppliers incurring additional costs that are passed 
on to the Company. These foregoing risks may adversely impact 
the Company, including its reputation, business, financial condition, 
operating results, cash flows or prospects. It is difficult to reasonably 
estimate the future impact of environmental matters, such as climate 
change and extreme weather events, including potential liabilities.
4.2  Ericsson incorporates AI technologies into certain products, 
­services and processes, which may present operational and 
­reputational risks.
Ericsson has incorporated and intends to continue to incorporate AI 
technologies into its products, services and processes. The market for 
such technologies is subject to rapid technological change, innovation, 
evolving industry standards, changing customer needs, requirements, 
and preferences. Ericsson’s success depends on its ability to continue 
to innovate and enhance existing products and services, expand offer-
ings, and anticipate and respond to the rapidly changing landscape 
and develop and introduce new offerings that will keep pace with 
technological and competitive developments. As with many innova-
tions, AI presents risks and challenges that could adversely impact 
Ericsson’s business. If Ericsson fails to keep pace with rapidly evolving 
technological developments in AI, its competitive position and busi-
ness results may suffer. The introduction of these technologies, par-
ticularly generative AI, into internal processes and new and existing 
product and service offerings may result in new or expanded risks and 
liabilities, including enhanced governmental or regulatory scrutiny, lit-
igation, compliance issues, ethical concerns, intellectual property, con-
fidentiality or security risks, as well as other risks that could adversely 
affect Ericsson’s reputation, business, operating results and financial 
condition. 
Ericsson may be unable to predict or fully mitigate the environ-
mental impacts associated with deploying and scaling AI capabili-
ties, including materially higher energy and water consumption and 
emissions from increased data center compute and cooling demands, 
higher lifecycle emissions across hardware and supply chains, and 
greater demand for renewable energy, which could increase the Com-
pany’s operating costs, impact the Company’s ability to achieve its Net 
Zero goal, expose the Company to evolving regulatory requirements 
and reporting obligations, and harm the Company’s reputation and 
brand if the Company’s mitigation measures prove inadequate.
Ericsson may be unsuccessful in identifying or resolving AI-related 
ethical and legal issues before they arise. Regulation of AI technology 
is rapidly changing, complicating both compliance and development 
efforts. AI-related issues, deficiencies and/or failures could give rise 
to legal and/or regulatory action, including with respect to proposed 
legislation regulating AI in certain jurisdictions, such as the European 
Union, which evolves from time to time, and as a result of new appli-
cations of existing data protection regulation, which could damage 
Ericsson’s reputation or otherwise materially harm its business. 
AI technologies can create accuracy issues, unintended biases, 
and discriminatory outcomes, or may create or rely on content that is 
inaccurate or flawed. If Ericsson fails to appropriately respond to this 
evolving landscape, or the recommendations, content, or analyses 
that AI applications produce are or are alleged to be deficient or inac-
curate, Ericsson could be subjected to competitive harm, potential 
legal liability, and brand or reputational harm. The legal and regula-
tory landscape surrounding AI technologies is rapidly evolving and 
uncertain, including in the areas of intellectual property, cybersecurity, 
and privacy and data protection. For example, there is uncertainty 
around the validity and enforceability of intellectual property rights 
related to the use, development, and deployment of AI technologies. 
Compliance with new or changing laws, regulations or industry stan-
dards relating to AI may impose significant operational costs and may 
limit Ericsson’s ability to develop, deploy or use AI technologies. There 
can be no assurance that the measures Ericsson has taken to mitigate 
the potential risks related to AI will be sufficient. Ericsson may also be 
exposed to these and other risks through the increased use of AI by 
ourits manufacturers, suppliers, and other business partners. Any of 
the above could result in a material adverse effect on Ericsson’s repu-
tation, business, operating results and financial condition.

5.3  Potential health risks related to radiofrequency electro-­
magnetic fields may subject Ericsson to various product liability 
claims and result in regulatory changes.
The mobile telecommunications industry is subject to claims that 
mobile devices and other equipment that generate radiofrequency 
electromagnetic fields may expose individuals to health risks. At pres-
ent, a substantial number of scientific reviews conducted by various 
independent research bodies have concluded that radiofrequency 
electromagnetic fields, when used at levels within the limits prescribed 
by public health authority safety standards and recommendations, 
cause no adverse effects to human health. However, the US Depart-
ment of Health and Human Services have announced plans to launch 
a new study on possible health effects of cell phone usage, and any 
perceived risk or new scientific findings of adverse health effects from 
mobile communication devices and equipment could adversely affect 
Ericsson through a reduction in sales or through liability claims. 
Although Ericsson’s products are designed to comply with currently 
applicable safety standards and regulations regarding radio frequency 
electromagnetic fields, the Company cannot guarantee that Ericsson 
will not become the subject of product liability claims. Ericsson also 
cannot guarantee that the Company will not be held liable for such 
claims or be required to comply with future changed regulatory 
requirements. Ericsson may, in addition, be affected by regulatory or 
other restrictions imposed on the Company’s customers use of radio 
equipment that may have a material adverse effect on Ericsson’s busi-
ness, operating results, financial condition, reputation and brand. 
Additionally, the US Securities Exchange Commission’s disclosure 
requirements regarding specified minerals (conflict minerals) could 
adversely affect the sourcing, availability and pricing of minerals used 
in the manufacture of certain of Ericsson’s products, which may have 
a material adverse effect on its business. In addition, since Ericsson’s 
supply chain is complex, the Company may not be able to sufficiently 
verify the origins for all these minerals contained in its products 
through the due diligence procedures that Ericsson implements, which 
may harm its reputation and its business. Ericsson may also encounter 
challenges if customers request that all Ericsson’s product compo-
nents be certified as ”conflict-free” or not have any exposure to cer-
tain regions. Ericsson acknowledges that similar challenges exist for 
other minerals and metals, outside the scope of the US Securities and 
Exchange Commission disclosure rule.

sustainable supply of certain raw materials that are to be designated 
strategic or critical, entered into force and may impact Ericsson’s cur-
rent supply chains in relation to the sourcing of certain materials, and 
such impact may therefore have an adverse effect on its business.

Revenue recognition from large contracts with customers
Ericsson generates revenues primarily from sales of hardware, soft-
ware, and services to its customers. The majority of these revenues 
are related to large multi-year framework agreements with customers 
which often include discount and incentive arrangements. The associ-
ated customers issue purchase orders under these framework agree-
ments that in combination constitute a contract and commitment to 
purchases of products and services over the duration of the agreement 
with the customer. These large contracts with customers may give rise 
to a risk of material misstatement due to incorrect amount and timing 
of revenue recognition for the respective obligation, that could have a 
material impact on the financial statements. 
Ericsson conducts an assessment at contract inception to deter-
mine which promised goods and services in a contract are distinct and 
accordingly identified as performance obligations. The amount and 
timing of revenue recognized is determined in relation to the individual 
performance obligations of the contract. 
Application of accounting standards for revenue recognition 
of large contracts with customers is associated with complexity in 
determining the amount and timing of revenue recognized in relation 
to individual elements of the contracts and involves inherent man-
agement judgment. We identified revenue recognition from large 
contracts with customers as a key audit matter due to the significant 
degree of audit effort, especially in evaluating the sufficiency of audit 
evidence, in performing audit procedures to evaluate the adherence to 
the accounting standards.
Our audit procedures related to the amount and timing of revenue 
recognized in relation to large contracts included, but were not limited 
to the following:
	
– We tested the effectiveness of the Company’s controls over reve-
nue recognition with particular focus on the controls related to the 
amount and timing of revenue recognition for each performance 
obligation within large contracts with customers.
	
– We tested a sample of large contracts with customers to assess 
management’s judgments related to the timing of recognition for 
each revenue obligation based on the contract.
	
– We tested a sample of revenue transactions related to large con-
tracts with customers recorded during the year by tracing them to 
supporting evidence of delivery and acceptance and assessed the 
revenue recorded in the period by comparing it to contract terms 
such as, delivery terms, transaction prices including, discount and 
incentive agreements
	
– We tested a sample of ongoing negotiations with existing customers 
and analyzed reversals of revenue subsequent to year end for indica-
tors of unrecorded discounts and concessions during the period.

In addition to our audit of the annual accounts and consolidated 
accounts, we have also audited the administration of the Board 
of Directors and the Managing Director of Telefonaktiebolaget LM 
Ericsson (publ) for the financial year January 1, 2025  – December 31, 
2025 and the proposed appropriations of the company’s profit or loss.
We recommend to the general meeting of shareholders that the 
profit to be appropriated in accordance with the proposal in the stat-
utory administration report and that the members of the Board of 
Directors and the Managing Director be discharged from liability for 
the financial year. 
Basis for Opinions
We conducted the audit in accordance with generally accepted audit-
ing standards in Sweden. Our responsibilities under those standards 
are further described in the Auditor’s Responsibilities section. We are 
independent of the parent company and the group in accordance 
with professional ethics for accountants in Sweden and have oth-
erwise fulfilled our ethical responsibilities in accordance with these 
requirements.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient 
and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinions.
Responsibilities of the Board of Directors and  
the Managing Director
The Board of Directors is responsible for the proposal for appropria-
tions of the company’s profit or loss. At the proposal of a dividend, this 
includes an assessment of whether the dividend is justifiable consid-
ering the requirements which the company's and the group’s type of 
operations, size and risks place on the size of the parent company's 
and the group’s equity, consolidation requirements, liquidity and posi-
tion in general.
The Board of Directors is responsible for the company’s organi-
zation and the administration of the company’s affairs. This includes 
among other things continuous assessment of the company’s and the 
group’s financial situation and ensuring that the company's organi-
zation is designed so that the accounting, management of assets and 
the company’s financial affairs otherwise are controlled in a reassur-
ing manner. The Managing Director shall manage the ongoing admin-
istration according to the Board of Directors’ guidelines and instruc-
tions and among other matters take measures that are necessary to 
fulfill the company’s accounting in accordance with law and handle 
the management of assets in a reassuring manner.
Auditor’s responsibility
Our objective concerning the audit of the administration, and thereby 
our opinion about discharge from liability, is to obtain audit evidence 
to assess with a reasonable degree of assurance whether any mem-
ber of the Board of Directors or the Managing Director in any material 
respect:
	
– has undertaken any action or been guilty of any omission which can 
give rise to liability to the company, or
	
– in any other way has acted in contravention of the Companies Act, 
the Annual Accounts Act or the Articles of Association.
Our objective concerning the audit of the proposed appropriations of 
the company’s profit or loss, and thereby our opinion about this, is to 
assess with reasonable degree of assurance whether the proposal is in 
accordance with the Companies Act.
Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, but is not a 
guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with generally 
accepted auditing standards in Sweden will always detect actions or 
omissions that can give rise to liability to the company, or that the pro-
posed appropriations of the company’s profit or loss are not in accor-
dance with the Companies Act.
As part of an audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing 
standards in Sweden, we exercise professional judgment and main-
tain professional scepticism throughout the audit. The examination of 
the administration and the proposed appropriations of the company’s 
profit or loss is based primarily on the audit of the accounts. Additional 
audit procedures performed are based on our professional judgment 
with starting point in risk and materiality. This means that we focus 
the examination on such actions, areas and relationships that are

Alternative performance measures
In this section, the Company presents its Alternative Performance 
Measures (APMs), which are not recognized measures of financial 
performance under IFRS. This section includes a reconciliation of the 
APM’s to the most directly reconcilable line items in the financial state-
ments. The presentation of APMs has limitations as analytical tools 
and should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for related 
financial measures prepared in accordance with IFRS.
APMs are presented to enhance an investor’s evaluation of ongoing 
operating results, to aid in forecasting future periods and to facilitate 
meaningful comparison of results between periods. 
Management uses these APMs to, among other things, evaluate 
ongoing operations in relation to historical results, for internal planning 
and forecasting purposes and in the calculation of certain performance- 
based compensation. APMs should not be viewed as substitutes for 
income statement or cash flow items computed in accordance with IFRS.
The definition of Return on capital employed (ROCE) and Capital 
turnover (CTO) have been updated and is based on a rolling average 
rather than an average of the beginning and the end of the period. 
Operating working capital has been added as an APM replacing 
Adjusted working capital. The Company believes the updated defini-
tions better reflect the underlying results of the Company’s operations 
over time.
The APMs presented in this report may differ from similarly titled 
measures used by other companies.

Definition
EBIT: Earnings (loss) before financial items and income tax. 
EBIT margin: EBIT as a percentage of net sales. 
Adjusted EBIT: EBIT excluding restructuring charges.
Adjusted EBIT margin: Adjusted EBIT as a percentage of net sales.
Adjusted EBIT excluding impairment of goodwill and intangible assets: EBIT excluding 
restructuring charges and impairment of goodwill and intangible assets.
Adjusted EBIT margin excluding impairment of goodwill and intangible assets  
as a percentage of net sales. 
Definition
EBITA: earnings (loss) before interest, income tax, amortizations and write-downs  
of acquired intangible assets (including goodwill).
EBITA margin: EBITA as a percentage of net sales.
Adjusted EBITA: EBITA excluding restructuring charges.
Adjusted EBITA margin: Adjusted EBITA as a percentage of net sales.
Reason to use
EBIT margin shows the EBIT in percentage of net sales. EBIT margin is a key internal 
measure as the Company believes that it provides users of the financial statements  
with a better understanding of the Group’s short- and long-term financial performance. 
The Company’s view is that adjusted EBIT margin excluding impairment of goodwill 
and intangible assets gives a fair view of the profitability of the ongoing business.
The Company decided to change the adjusted EBIT excluding impairment of 
goodwill to also exclude the impairment of intangible assets. The comparison years 
have been updated accordingly.
Reason to use
Amortizations and write-downs of intangible assets are normally non-cash items in 
the income statement. EBITA margin gives an indication of the financial performance 
without the impact from acquired companies. The Company’s view is that adjusted 
EBITA margin gives a fair view of the profitability of the ongoing business.
Additionally, Ericsson provides forward-looking targets for adjusted EBITA margin and 
Free cash flow before M&A as a percentage of net sales, which are non-IFRS financial 
measures. Ericsson has not provided quantitative reconciliation of these targets to 
the most directly comparable IFRS measures because certain information needed to 
reconcile these non-IFRS financial measures to the most comparable IFRS financial 
measures are dependent on specific items or impacts that are not yet determined, are 
subject to incarcerating and variability in timing and amount due to their nature, are 
outside of Ericsson’s control or cannot be predicted, including items and impacts such 
as currency exchange rate changes, acquisitions and disposals, and charges such 
as impairments or acquisition related charges. Accordingly, reconciliations of these 
non-IFRS forward-looking financial measures to the most directly comparable IFRS 
financial measures are not available without unreasonable efforts. Such unavailable 
reconciling items could significantly impact our results of operations and financial 
condition.

Definition

Definition
Cash and cash equivalents plus interest-bearing securities (current and non-current).
Reason to use
Free cash flow before M&A represents the cash that the Company generates after 
capital expenditures, other investments and repayment of lease liabilities. The 
Company believes that free cash flow before M&A is a good way of reflecting the cash 
flows generated by the Company that can be used to expand the business, invest in 
subsidiaries, pay dividends and reduce debt.
Free cash flow after M&A represents the cash that the Company generates after 
capital expenditures, other investments, repayment of lease liabilities and acquisitions/
divestments of subsidiaries. The Company believes that free cash flow after M&A is a 
good way of reflecting the cash flows generated by the Company that can be used to 
expand the business, pay dividends and reduce debt. 
Free cash flow before M&A as a percentage of net sales is used by the Company as 
one of the long-term targets, as it reflects the Company’s ability to convert net sales into 
free cash flow.

Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson’s Annual 
General Meeting 2026 will be held on 
Tuesday, March 31, 2026 at 2 p.m. CET at 
Ericsson’s premises: Open Box, Grönlands­
gatan 8, Kista/Stockholm, Sweden. 
Shareholders are also able to exercise  
their voting rights by post before the meeting.
Information on registration and notice of 
participation, on how shareholders will be 
able to exercise their voting rights, and on 
proxies and assistants is found in the notice 
of the Annual General Meeting. Information 
is also available on the Company’s website 
www.ericsson.com.
Capital Allocation
The Ericsson Board of Directors has under-
taken a review of the capital allocation priori-
ties and balance sheet structure during 2025. 
The capital allocation principles are; (1) 
Maintain technology leadership and ensure 
strong customer confidence through contin-
ued investments in R&D, even during periods 
of increased market volatility or low visibility; 
(2) Stable to progressive ordinary dividends; 
(3) Selective inorganic investments to com-
plement the existing product portfolio and/ 
or market footprint; and (4) Ensure capital 
discipline through distributing excess cash  
to shareholders.
Ericsson strives for a solid net cash posi-
tion over time to secure its top priorities of 
technology leadership and customer con-
fidence, while remaining committed to an 
investment grade credit rating.
Shareholder information
Based on the review and the full-year 
2025 results, and in line with the updated 
capital allocation principles, the Board has 
concluded there is excess cash available to 
distribute to shareholders.
The Board of Directors will propose to the 
Annual General Meeting (AGM) an ordinary 
dividend of SEK 3.00 (2.85) per share. The 
dividend is proposed to be paid in two install-
ments, SEK 1.50 per share with the record date 
April 2, 2026 (payment date April 9, 2026), 
and SEK 1.50 per share with the record date 
September 29, 2026 (payment date October 2, 
2026). The proposed dividend takes into con-
sideration 2025 earnings, the balance sheet, 
future business plans, and expected eco-
nomic developments. For the Parent Compa-
ny’s treasury shares of Class B, no dividend 
will be distributed.
Ericsson’s Board of Directors will further 
propose to the AGM to authorize the Board 
to initiate a share buyback program to repur-
chase shares, with purchases expected to 
begin following the publication of the Q1 
2026 report. The proposed program targets 
to return up to SEK 15 billion of cash to share-
holders over the period extending to the 2027 
AGM at the latest, with a formal mandate to 
buy back a maximum of 10% of shares out-
standing. The share repurchase is proposed 
to include Class B shares traded on Nasdaq 
Stockholm. The repurchased shares are 
expected to be canceled or partially used  
to fund approved LTV programs.
In total, the proposals amount to a 
potential distribution to shareholders of 
up to SEK 25.0 billion for the financial year 
2025. Adjusted for the proposed share-
holder distributions, the net cash position at 
year end 2025 remains at a solid level when 
considering future investments to maintain 
technology leadership.
